notes.title: Floci Lakehouse: from messy reviews to queryable Parquet
notes.summary: An intuitive guide to validation, Bronze/Silver/Gold storage, running on local Floci, analytical engines and the path to vector retrieval.
notes.content:
# Floci Lakehouse: from messy reviews to queryable Parquet

`floci-lakehouse` turns JSONL review records into typed Parquet datasets stored in
Floci S3. It keeps rejected lines for inspection, produces category/year summaries,
and compares Polars, DuckDB and Pandas on the same analytical workload.

Think of it as a small receiving warehouse: Bronze keeps the delivery exactly as
it arrived, validation inspects each item, Silver shelves the accepted records,
quarantine retains rejected items with a reason, and Gold holds prepared reports.

## The whole journey

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Input[Local review JSONL] --> Bronze[Bronze: original bytes in Floci S3]
    Bronze --> Reader[Python: bounded line reader]
    Reader --> Validate[Pydantic: validate and normalize]
    Validate -->|Accepted| Arrow[Arrow: fixed column types]
    Validate -->|Rejected| Quarantine[Quarantine: line and structured errors]
    Arrow --> Silver[Silver: partitioned ZSTD Parquet]
    Silver --> Complete[Completion manifest after all writes succeed]
    Quarantine --> Complete
    Complete --> Polars[Polars: lazy scan and aggregation]
    Polars --> Gold[Gold: category and year summaries]
    Complete --> SQL[DuckDB: SQL over Silver]
    Complete --> Bench[Polars / DuckDB / Pandas comparison]
```

The completion manifest acts like a signed packing list. Downstream commands
require it so that partially written files are not mistaken for a completed run.
It is a completion convention, not an atomic transaction across S3 objects.

## Where Floci fits

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Host[Your computer]
        CLI[uv run lakehouse]
        Python[Validation and Arrow writes]
        Engines[Polars / DuckDB / Pandas]
        CLI --> Python
        CLI --> Engines
    end
    subgraph Container[Docker container]
        Floci[Floci S3-compatible API: port 4566]
        Volume[Persistent floci-data volume]
        Floci --> Volume
    end
    Python <-->|S3 requests| Floci
    Engines <-->|Parquet reads and writes| Floci
```

Floci supplies the local object-storage API. Python and the analytical engines run
on your computer; Floci does not execute these jobs. This project does not launch
Spark, Glue jobs, or an automatic event-driven pipeline. Each CLI command explicitly
starts one stage.

The Compose service exposes `127.0.0.1:4566`. Each client receives the endpoint,
region, dummy credentials and path-style addressing explicitly. Successful boto3
access alone does not establish that Arrow, Polars and DuckDB can all access S3.

## Follow one review

Imagine a Books review with a rating of `"4"`, a timestamp in Unix milliseconds,
and a null text field. The validator accepts the numeric string, retains the
permitted null, and derives the UTC partition year. Arrow then writes consistently
typed columns even when a batch begins with null values.

A rating outside 1–5, missing required identifier, malformed JSON or invalid
category instead produces a quarantine record. That record identifies the source
and line and explains the failure. Oversized lines retain a bounded prefix in
quarantine; the complete original input remains in Bronze.

| Layer | Default location | Why keep it? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bronze | `s3://lakehouse-bronze/uploads/<uuid>/<filename>` | Inspect or reprocess the original bytes. |
| Silver | `s3://lakehouse-silver/runs/<id>/reviews/category=Books/year=2023/` | Query validated rows with stable column types. |
| Quarantine | `s3://lakehouse-quarantine/runs/<id>/batch-000000.jsonl` | Investigate rejected records without losing their context. |
| Gold | `s3://lakehouse-gold/runs/<id>/all/summary.parquet` | Reuse category/year counts, average ratings and vote totals. |

Hive partition directories carry `category` and `year`; readers reconstruct those
columns from paths. Parquet stores the remaining columns in compressed columnar
form. A query selecting ratings does not need to materialize all review text.

Every physical input line must have one outcome:

```text
valid Silver rows + quarantine rows = total input lines
```

Duplicates are preserved. A second ingestion with a new run ID creates another
independent run; it does not deduplicate or merge with the previous run.

## Run against local Floci

Prerequisites: Python 3.12–3.14, uv, Docker 23+ and Docker Compose v2. Start in
the `floci-lakehouse/` directory. Dependency installation needs network access.

```bash
uv sync --python 3.12
cp .env.example .env
docker compose up -d
docker compose ps
```

Copy the example only when creating your configuration; preserve an existing
`.env`. Its local storage settings are:

```dotenv
AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=http://localhost:4566
AWS_REGION=us-east-1
AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=test
AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=test
```

Use dummy credentials for this local exercise. The CLI loads `.env` only when
`--env-file` is supplied.

Create the buckets, ingest the fixture, then run the two analytical paths:

```bash
uv run lakehouse --env-file .env bootstrap
uv run lakehouse --env-file .env ingest data/fixtures/mixed_reviews.jsonl --run-id demo
uv run lakehouse --env-file .env transform --run-id demo
uv run lakehouse --env-file .env query --run-id demo
```

Expected fixture reconciliation is **50 physical lines = 40 valid + 10 rejected**.
The ingest command prints counts and S3 locations. Transform prints the Gold URI;
query prints category/year counts from Silver. These are expected outcomes from
the implementation, not a claim of a verified live run.

The run ID is reserved before ingestion. For another attempt use `demo-2` or omit
`--run-id` to generate a UUID. A failed run keeps its reservation and partial
artifacts; it cannot be resumed by reusing the ID.

If port 4566 is already occupied, start this project's service on another port:

```bash
FLOCI_PORT=4568 docker compose up -d
```

Then set `AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=http://localhost:4568` in `.env` before running the CLI.
Stop the service with `docker compose down`; the named volume retains its data.

## Ask a question, then compare engines

```bash
uv run lakehouse --env-file .env query --run-id demo \
  --sql "SELECT category, avg(rating) AS average_rating FROM reviews GROUP BY category" \
  --limit 20
uv run lakehouse --env-file .env bench --run-id demo \
  --repeats 3 --output data/benchmarks/demo.json
```

DuckDB exposes the completed Silver dataset as `reviews`. Its first S3 query
needs network access to install `httpfs`; later runs reuse the extension cache.

Polars builds a lazy scan so projection and filtering can be pushed toward the
read. DuckDB expresses the work in SQL. Pandas provides an eager Arrow-backed
baseline that materializes the selected data and must fit in RAM.

The benchmark applies `rating >= 3` and compares category/year counts, mean ratings
and helpful-vote sums. It fully consumes each result and checks equivalence before
reporting timings. That filter differs from the all-rating Gold transform: compare
matching workloads when interpreting totals.

Batch thresholds limit retained input and flush size, not total process memory.
Arrow buffers and Python objects add overhead; aggregation state grows with group
cardinality. Benchmark cache effects, thread defaults and sampled RSS also limit
what a single measurement can prove.

## How this connects to vector embedding and retrieval

This project supplies the data-quality foundation for retrieval. Validated text,
source identifiers and metadata can become inputs to a later embedding pipeline.
It currently implements analytical storage and querying, not embeddings or vector
search.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Silver[Implemented: validated Silver reviews] --> Prepare[Future: select text and assign stable document IDs]
    Prepare --> Chunk[Future: chunk text with provenance]
    Chunk --> Embed[Future: generate versioned embeddings]
    Embed --> Index[Future: build vector index]
    Index --> Retrieve[Future: retrieve text and source metadata]
```

That future pipeline should define how null/empty text is handled, how duplicate
reviews become document identities, and which embedding model and chunking version
created each vector. Stable provenance lets a search result lead back to the exact
source record. Those decisions are not yet implemented here.

## Verify and troubleshoot

```bash
uv run pytest tests/unit
uv run pytest tests/integration -m integration
uv run ruff check .
uv run ruff format --check .
uv run mypy
uv build
```

Integration tests normally start an isolated Floci container. To use an existing
local service instead:

```bash
FLOCI_TEST_ENDPOINT=http://localhost:4566 uv run pytest tests/integration -m integration
```

The tests create uniquely named buckets and clean up only their own test buckets.

| Symptom | Next check |
| --- | --- |
| Connection refused | Check `docker compose ps`, host port and `.env` endpoint. |
| Run ID already exists | Use a new ID; inspect the previous run separately. |
| Files exist but queries refuse the run | Check whether ingestion completed and wrote its manifest. |
| Amazon rows lack a category | Supply `--category All_Beauty` when ingesting that source. |
| DuckDB cannot query S3 | Check httpfs installation and DuckDB's endpoint settings. |
| Counts differ between Gold and benchmark | Account for the benchmark's `rating >= 3` filter. |

Recorded implementation evidence in `VERIFICATION.md` dated November 13, 2026
reports 52 passing unit tests, lint/format checks, Python syntax compilation and
package builds. Dependency installation and Docker access were blocked; live
Floci ingestion, engine integration, installed CLI execution, mypy and benchmarks
remain unverified. No live performance measurements are reported here.

For source navigation, start with `src/lakehouse/cli.py`, then
`pipelines/bronze_to_silver.py`, `contracts/models.py`,
`pipelines/silver_to_gold.py` and `analytics/duckdb_engine.py` inside the package.
The repository's `README.md`, `ARCHITECTURE.md`, `code-map.md` and
`VERIFICATION.md` provide commands, boundaries, navigation and execution evidence.

notes.title: Pooling Layers in SentenceTransformers
notes.content:
# Pooling Layers in SentenceTransformers
**Intuition, Selection Criteria, Attention Mask Mechanics, and LLM Last-Token (EOS) Pooling**

---

## 1. The Core Problem Pooling Solves
When text passes through a Transformer backbone (such as BERT, MPNet, or Qwen), the network outputs a 2D matrix of shape `(sequence_length, embedding_dimension)`:
* A **5-word sentence** produces a `(7, 768)` matrix (5 words + `[CLS]` + `[SEP]`).
* A **50-word paragraph** produces a `(52, 768)` matrix.

Vector databases and similarity metrics (like Cosine Similarity or Dot Product) cannot directly compare a `(7, 768)` matrix against a `(52, 768)` matrix. The **Pooling Layer** collapses the variable `sequence_length` dimension down to `1`, converting both inputs into identical `(1, 768)` fixed-size vectors.

```text
Input Tokens:     [CLS]    "Dogs"   "love"   "parks"   [SEP]
                    │         │        │        │        │
Token Vectors:   [0.1..]   [0.8..]  [0.4..]  [0.9..]  [0.2..]   (5 x 768 Matrix)
                    │         │        │        │        │
                    └─────────┴────────┼────────┴────────┘
                                       ▼
                              [ POOLING LAYER ]
                                       │
                                       ▼
Sentence Vector:            [0.48, 0.52, ..., 0.31]             (1 x 768 Vector)
```

---

## 2. The Three Primary Pooling Strategies

### A. Mean Pooling (The Modern Default)
* **How It Works:** Averages all token vectors across the entire sequence while ignoring `[PAD]` (padding) tokens via the attention mask.
* **Core Intuition:** Treats the sentence as a balanced democratic committee where every word contributes equally to the final representation. No single word dominates unless the overall theme reinforces it.
* **When to Use It:**
  * General-purpose semantic search, clustering, and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG).
  * Comparing full sentences or paragraphs where overall context matters more than isolated buzzwords.
  * Whenever deploying standard SBERT models (`all-MiniLM-L6-v2`, `all-mpnet-base-v2`, `intfloat/e5-*`).
* **Concrete Example:**
  * *Sentence:* `"The server crashed because the memory buffer overflowed."`
  * *Why Mean Pooling Wins:* It blends `"server"`, `"crashed"`, `"memory"`, `"buffer"`, and `"overflowed"` into one unified technical concept, matching queries like `"System outage due to RAM exhaustion"` even with zero exact keyword overlap.

### B. `[CLS]`-Token Pooling
* **How It Works:** Discards every individual word vector and keeps **only the very first vector** corresponding to the special `[CLS]` (Classification) token prepended at index `0`.
* **Core Intuition:** Acts like an executive summary written by a note-taker. During contrastive pre-training, the model is explicitly forced to funnel the entire meaning of the sequence into that single front token.
* **When to Use It:**
  * **Only** when using models explicitly trained with `[CLS]` pooling (such as **BGE** models like `BAAI/bge-large-en-v1.5`, **Snowflake Arctic Embed**, or **DPR**).
  * **Never** apply `[CLS]` pooling to a raw, un-tuned BERT model—raw BERT's `[CLS]` vector is only trained for Next Sentence Prediction and performs worse than averaging uncontextualized word embeddings.
* **Concrete Example:**
  * *Sentence:* `"Is a passport required for domestic flights in Canada?"`
  * *Why `[CLS]` Pooling Wins (on BGE models):* Self-attention heads actively route the combined intent (`requirement` + `passport` + `domestic flight` + `Canada`) directly into token index `0`.

### C. Max Pooling
* **How It Works:** Scans down each of the embedding columns (dimensions) independently and picks the **single highest numerical activation** across all tokens in the sentence.
* **Core Intuition:** Acts like a highlighter marker or a sensitive alarm bell. If even one word triggers an extreme spike in dimension #412 (e.g., a feature sensitive to "cybersecurity threats" or "legal liability"), that peak signal survives regardless of how long or diluted the surrounding paragraph is.
* **When to Use It:**
  * **Short-to-Long Asymmetric Matching:** Locating a specific fact or entity buried inside a noisy, multi-sentence paragraph.
  * **Anomaly, Toxicity, or Red-Flag Detection:** Where one critical term must not be washed out by 40 neutral words.
  * **Hybrid Concatenations:** Combined with Mean Pooling (`Mean + Max` = 1536 dimensions) in custom text classification pipelines.
* **Concrete Example:**
  * *Paragraph:* `"The quarterly meeting covered office snacks, parking passes, printer maintenance, and a critical ransomware breach in the billing database."`
  * *Why Max Pooling Helps:* Mean pooling dilutes `"ransomware breach"` with mundane terms like `"snacks"` and `"printer"`. Max pooling preserves the extreme activation spike from `"ransomware"`.

---

## 3. Side-by-Side Comparison Matrix

| Pooling Method | Mathematical Operation | Best Use Case | Primary Weakness | Famous Models Using It |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Mean Pooling** | Average of all non-padding token vectors | General semantic similarity, clustering, and standard RAG | Dilutes rare keywords inside very long, noisy paragraphs | `all-MiniLM-L6-v2`, `all-mpnet-base-v2`, `intfloat/e5-*` |
| **`[CLS]` Pooling** | Extracts vector at index `0` (`[CLS]` token) | High-speed retrieval on models explicitly trained for `[CLS]` | Severe accuracy drop if applied to non-`[CLS]` models | `BAAI/bge-*`, `Snowflake/snowflake-arctic-embed-*` |
| **Max Pooling** | Maximum value per dimension across all tokens | Spotting specific signals/entities in noisy text; classification | Noisy on general similarity; ignores overall sentence flow | `InferSent` (historic), custom `Mean+Max` classifiers |
| **Last-Token (EOS)** | Extracts vector at the final non-padding token | Decoder-only LLM embedders with causal attention masks | Cannot see future tokens; requires causal LLM backbones | `Qwen3-Embedding`, `Mistral-Embed`, `NV-Embed` |

---

## 4. Deep Dive: How Attention Masks Protect Mean Pooling Math

When encoding a batch of sentences of different lengths on a GPU, tensors must be rectangular. Shorter sentences are padded with dummy `[PAD]` tokens to match the longest sentence in the batch.

### The Corruption Risk Without Attention Masks
Suppose a batch contains a 3-token sentence (`"AI is fast"`) and a 6-token sentence (`"Deep learning models process data quickly"`):
* Without masking, `"AI is fast"` becomes `["AI", "is", "fast", "[PAD]", "[PAD]", "[PAD]"]`.
* `[PAD]` tokens still pass through the Transformer layers and produce non-zero garbage vectors.
* A naive average across all 6 positions divides by `6` instead of `3` and mixes 50% padding noise into the final sentence embedding. Two identical sentences encoded in different batch sizes would produce completely different vectors.

### How Mask-Weighted Mean Pooling Fixes It
The tokenizer generates an **Attention Mask** containing `1` for real tokens and `0` for `[PAD]` tokens:

```text
Tokens:          ["AI",   "is",   "fast", "[PAD]", "[PAD]", "[PAD]"]
Attention Mask:  [  1,      1,      1,       0,       0,       0   ]

Step 1: Broadcast Mask to Embedding Dimensions (e.g., 768 dims)
        Real Token Vector  * 1  = Original Vector Kept
        [PAD] Token Vector * 0  = Zeroed Out Completely [0.0, 0.0, ...]

Step 2: Sum Masked Vectors Across Sequence
        Sum = Vector("AI") + Vector("is") + Vector("fast") + 0 + 0 + 0

Step 3: Divide by Sum of Attention Mask (Not Total Sequence Length!)
        Valid Token Count = 1 + 1 + 1 + 0 + 0 + 0 = 3
        Final Sentence Vector = Sum / 3
```

* **Numerical Safety (`clamp(min=1e-9)`):** In PyTorch implementations, the denominator is clamped to a tiny positive value (`1e-9`) so an empty string with an all-zero mask never triggers a `ZeroDivisionError` (`NaN`).
* **Effect on Max Pooling:** Before taking the maximum across tokens, masked `[PAD]` positions are set to `-1e9` (negative infinity) so a padding vector can never beat a real token's activation.

---

## 5. Deep Dive: Last-Token (EOS) Pooling in Modern LLM Embedders

Classic encoders (BERT, RoBERTa, MPNet) are **bidirectional**—every token looks both left and right simultaneously, allowing token `0` (`[CLS]`) or the average of all tokens to capture full context.

However, modern high-capacity embedding models (`Qwen3-Embedding`, `Mistral-Embed`, `GritLM`, `E5-Mistral`) are built on **decoder-only Large Language Models (LLMs)** that use **Causal (Uni-Directional) Attention**.

### Why Mean and `[CLS]` Pooling Fail on Causal LLMs
In a causal LLM, token `i` can only attend to tokens `0` through `i` (past tokens). It is strictly blind to future tokens:
* Token `0` (`[BOS]` or the first word) has **zero awareness** of the rest of the sentence. Using `[CLS]`/first-token pooling captures nothing beyond the first word.
* Mean pooling averages early tokens (which lack full context) with late tokens, diluting the rich global representation built up at the end of the sequence.

### How Last-Token (EOS) Pooling Works
Because causal attention flows strictly from left to right, **only the very last real token** (typically the End-Of-Sequence `<|endoftext|>` or `</s>` token) has attended to every single preceding word in the prompt:

```text
Causal Attention Flow (Left-to-Right Only):

Token 1: "The"     ──► Sees: ["The"] (Blind to rest)
Token 2: "server"  ──► Sees: ["The", "server"]
Token 3: "crashed" ──► Sees: ["The", "server", "crashed"]
Token 4: "</s>"    ──► Sees: ["The", "server", "crashed", "</s>"]  ◄── EXTRACTED HERE!
                              (100% Full Sentence Context)
```

### Critical Padding Rule for Last-Token Pooling
* **Left-Padding vs. Right-Padding:** When batching sequences of different lengths for a Last-Token Pooling model, **left-padding** is strongly preferred (`[PAD] [PAD] The server crashed </s>`). With left-padding, the final real token always sits cleanly at index `-1` (`embeddings[:, -1]`).
* **Right-Padding Index Lookup:** If right-padding is used (`The server crashed </s> [PAD] [PAD]`), the pooling layer must calculate the exact index of the last `1` in each row's attention mask (`sequence_lengths = attention_mask.sum(dim=1) - 1`) rather than blindly slicing index `-1`.

---

## 6. Golden Rule & Complete Code Inspection

**Never manually swap the pooling method of a pre-trained model.** A model's transformer weights are tightly calibrated to whichever pooling layer was active during contrastive training.

```python
import torch
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer, models

# 1. Inspect the active pooling configuration of any pre-trained model
model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")
print(model[1])  # Prints: Pooling({'word_embedding_dimension': 384, 'pooling_mode_mean_tokens': True, ...})

# 2. Manual PyTorch Implementation of Mask-Weighted Mean Pooling
def mean_pooling(token_embeddings: torch.Tensor, attention_mask: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    # Expand mask from [batch, seq_len] to [batch, seq_len, hidden_dim]
    input_mask_expanded = attention_mask.unsqueeze(-1).expand(token_embeddings.size()).float()
    # Zero out [PAD] vectors and sum real tokens
    sum_embeddings = torch.sum(token_embeddings * input_mask_expanded, dim=1)
    # Count real tokens per sentence (clamped to avoid division by zero)
    sum_mask = torch.clamp(input_mask_expanded.sum(dim=1), min=1e-9)
    return sum_embeddings / sum_mask

# 3. Manual PyTorch Implementation of Last-Token (EOS) Pooling (works with right or left padding)
def last_token_pooling(last_hidden_states: torch.Tensor, attention_mask: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    left_padding = (attention_mask[:, -1].sum() == attention_mask.shape[0])
    if left_padding:
        return last_hidden_states[:, -1]
    sequence_lengths = attention_mask.sum(dim=1) - 1
    batch_size = last_hidden_states.shape[0]
    return last_hidden_states[torch.arange(batch_size, device=last_hidden_states.device), sequence_lengths]

# 4. Building a Custom Hybrid Mean + Max Pooling Model in SentenceTransformers
word_embedding_model = models.Transformer("bert-base-uncased", max_seq_length=256)
pooling_model = models.Pooling(
    word_embedding_model.get_word_embedding_dimension(),
    pooling_mode_mean_tokens=True,
    pooling_mode_cls_tokens=False,
    pooling_mode_max_tokens=True,
    pooling_mode_lasttoken=False
)
custom_model = SentenceTransformer(modules=[word_embedding_model, pooling_model])
print("Combined Output Dimension:", custom_model.get_sentence_embedding_dimension())  # 768 * 2 = 1536
```

notes.content:
# OAuth 2.0, OpenID Connect (OIDC) and Auth0

Modern identity and access management relies on a layered architecture. Rather than competing against one another, **OAuth 2.0**, **OpenID Connect (OIDC)**, and **Auth0** work together as a unified stack. This reference guide explains how these components connect, the roles involved, token structures, grant types, security mechanisms, and the complete authentication handshake—all without relying on external dependencies.

---

## 1. The Three-Layer Architecture & Conceptual Link

To understand how modern login and API security work, view the ecosystem as a three-tier stack consisting of a **foundation**, an **extension**, and a **managed platform**.

![image.png](/api/notes/oauth-2-0-openid-connect-oidc-and-auth0/assets/image-70ac99936c907d875dd39a24.png)

### Summary of Each Layer
1. **OAuth 2.0 (Delegated Authorization):** Created to solve the "valet key" problem of the web. Before OAuth 2.0, an application needing access to a user's cloud contacts or calendar required the user's actual username and password. OAuth 2.0 replaces password sharing with scoped, revocable **Access Tokens**. However, raw OAuth 2.0 only deals with permissions; it has no standardized way to tell an application who logged in.
2. **OpenID Connect / OIDC (Authentication):** Because developers kept inventing insecure workarounds to use OAuth 2.0 for user login, the OpenID Foundation created OIDC as a thin, standardized identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0. When an OAuth 2.0 request includes the `openid` scope, OIDC activates and returns an **ID Token** proving the user's identity.
3. **Auth0 (The Implementation Engine):** Building an OAuth 2.0 and OIDC server from scratch requires complex cryptography, key rotation, token signing, and brute-force protection. Auth0 is a cloud Identity-as-a-Service (IDaaS) platform that acts as the central engine executing these protocols out of the box.

---

## 2. The Four Core Roles (and Terminology Mapping)

Every OAuth 2.0 and OIDC transaction involves four distinct actors. While the physical entities remain identical, OIDC assigns specialized names to highlight identity verification over resource delegation.

| Conceptual Role | OAuth 2.0 Term | OpenID Connect (OIDC) Term | Concrete Example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **The Human User** | **Resource Owner** | **End-User** | A person logging into a project management web app. |
| **The Application** | **Client** | **Relying Party (RP)** | A React Single-Page App (SPA), iOS app, or Node.js backend requesting user profile data and API access. |
| **The Security Hub** | **Authorization Server** | **OpenID Provider (OP)** | **Auth0** (specifically, an Auth0 Tenant) validating credentials, enforcing MFA, and minting tokens. |
| **The Protected Data** | **Resource Server** | **Resource Server** | A protected backend REST or GraphQL API (e.g., `/api/invoices`) that validates Access Tokens before returning data. |

### Client Types: Confidential vs. Public
OAuth 2.0 classifies **Clients (Relying Parties)** into two security categories based on their ability to keep secrets safe:
* **Confidential Clients:** Applications running on a secure backend server (e.g., Python, Java, Node.js, .NET). Because end-users cannot inspect server source code or memory, these clients can safely store a `client_secret`.
* **Public Clients:** Applications running on untrusted devices where code is exposed to the user (e.g., browser-based Single-Page Applications or native mobile apps). Because any secret embedded in JavaScript or a mobile binary can be extracted, public clients **must never** use a `client_secret` and instead rely on **PKCE**.

---

## 3. Tokens & Scopes: Keys, Passports, and Claims

When an authentication and authorization handshake completes, Auth0 issues tokens. Understanding the strict boundary between **ID Tokens** and **Access Tokens** is critical for system security.

### Comparison of the Three Token Types

| Token Type | Protocol | Format | Intended Audience | Primary Purpose |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **ID Token** | OIDC Only | Always a **JWT** (JSON Web Token) | The **Client** (Relying Party) | Proves the user authenticated. Used by the frontend/client to read user profile attributes and establish a local session. **Never send to an API.** |
| **Access Token** | OAuth 2.0 | **JWT** or Opaque String | The **Resource Server** (API) | Authorizes API requests. Carries permissions (`scopes`) and audience (`aud`). The Client treats it as an opaque string and attaches it to HTTP headers. |
| **Refresh Token** | OAuth 2.0 | Opaque String | The **Authorization Server** (Auth0) | Long-lived credential stored securely by the Client to obtain fresh Access Tokens without prompting the user to log in again. |

### Inside a Decoded JWT (JSON Web Token)
Both ID Tokens and modern Access Tokens are typically formatted as **JWTs**, consisting of three Base64URL-encoded parts separated by dots (`Header.Payload.Signature`).

1. **Header:** Specifies the signing algorithm (e.g., `RS256`) and the Key ID (`kid`) used to verify the signature.
2. **Payload (Claims):** Contains key-value statements about the user or permissions:
   * `iss` (Issuer): The Auth0 tenant URL that minted the token (e.g., `https://example-tenant.us.auth0.com/`).
   * `sub` (Subject): The unique identifier for the user (e.g., `auth0|64f8a9b2c1d0`).
   * `aud` (Audience): Who the token is intended for. In an ID Token, this is the `client_id`. In an Access Token, this is the API identifier (e.g., `https://api.example.com`).
   * `exp` / `iat`: Expiration timestamp and Issued-At timestamp.
   * `scope`: Space-separated list of granted permissions in an Access Token (e.g., `openid profile email read:reports`).
3. **Signature:** Created by Auth0 using its private cryptographic key. The Client and Resource Server verify this signature using Auth0's public keys published at `https://<TENANT_DOMAIN>/.well-known/jwks.json`.

### Essential OIDC & OAuth Scopes
* `openid`: **Mandatory** to trigger OIDC. Tells Auth0 to return an ID Token.
* `profile`: Requests basic user claims (`name`, `family_name`, `given_name`, `picture`).
* `email`: Requests `email` and `email_verified` claims.
* `offline_access`: Requests a **Refresh Token** so the application can renew access in the background.
* Custom API Scopes (e.g., `write:orders`, `delete:users`): Defined inside Auth0 to govern fine-grained access to a Resource Server.

---

## 4. Front Channel vs. Back Channel Communication

To prevent tokens from being intercepted in browser history, logs, or malicious extensions, OAuth 2.0 separates traffic across two distinct network channels:

* **Front Channel:** Communication passing through the **User-Agent (Web Browser)** via HTTP redirects (`302 Found`) and URL query parameters. Because browser URLs are visible to plugins, proxies, and browser history, sensitive tokens should **never** travel over the Front Channel. Only short-lived, single-use **Authorization Codes** use this path.
* **Back Channel:** Direct, server-to-server HTTPS calls between the **Client** (or Resource Server) and **Auth0**. Because traffic never touches the browser, the Back Channel is used to exchange the Authorization Code for actual **ID, Access, and Refresh Tokens**.

---

## 5. Complete Sequence Diagram: Authorization Code Flow with PKCE

The **Authorization Code Flow with PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange)** is the universal security standard for web apps, Single-Page Applications (SPAs), and mobile apps. PKCE prevents "Authorization Code Interception Attacks" by proving that the application exchanging the code is the exact same application that initiated the login.

![image_15009143.jpg](/api/notes/oauth-2-0-openid-connect-oidc-and-auth0/assets/image-15009143-df16c43690ebe79f3caa6a1a.jpg)

### Step-by-Step Handshake Breakdown
1. **Login Initiation:** The End-User clicks the login button inside the Client application.
2. **PKCE Secret Generation:** The Client generates a cryptographically random string called the `code_verifier`. It then computes a SHA-256 hash of that string, producing the `code_challenge`.
3. **Authorization Request (Front Channel):** The Client redirects the browser to Auth0's `/authorize` endpoint, passing its `client_id`, the `redirect_uri`, requested `scopes` (including `openid`), a random `state` parameter (to prevent Cross-Site Request Forgery / CSRF), and the `code_challenge`.
4. **Authentication & Consent:** Auth0 displays its hosted login interface (Universal Login). The user enters credentials (and completes Multi-Factor Authentication if configured) and consents to requested scopes.
5. **Authorization Code Return (Front Channel):** Auth0 redirects the browser back to the Client's pre-approved `redirect_uri` with a short-lived, single-use `code` and the untouched `state` parameter. The Client verifies that the returned `state` matches the one it originally sent.
6. **Token Exchange (Back Channel):** The Client sends a direct, server-to-server `POST` request to Auth0's `/oauth/token` endpoint containing the `code`, `client_id`, `redirect_uri`, and the plain-text `code_verifier` generated in Step 2 (plus `client_secret` if the Client is a confidential backend server).
7. **Cryptographic Verification:** Auth0 hashes the incoming `code_verifier` with SHA-256 and confirms it matches the `code_challenge` stored during Step 3. Even if an attacker intercepted the `code` in Step 5, they cannot exchange it without the `code_verifier`.
8. **Token Issuance:** Auth0 responds with a JSON payload containing the **ID Token**, **Access Token**, and (if `offline_access` was requested) a **Refresh Token**.
9. **Session Creation:** The Client validates the ID Token's signature and claims (`iss`, `aud`, `exp`) and establishes an authenticated user session.
10. **UI Update:** The Client displays the user's profile name and avatar extracted from the ID Token.
11. **Protected API Call:** When the Client needs protected data, it calls the Resource Server and attaches the Access Token inside the HTTP header: `Authorization: Bearer <ACCESS_TOKEN>`.
12. **API Token Verification:** The Resource Server validates the Access Token's signature against Auth0's public JWKS keys, checks that `aud` matches its own API identifier, verifies `exp` has not passed, and confirms the `scope` permits the requested action.
13. **Data Delivery:** The Resource Server executes the business logic and returns the protected data.

---

## 6. Choosing the Right OAuth 2.0 Grant Type

While Authorization Code + PKCE handles interactive user logins, OAuth 2.0 provides specialized flows ("Grant Types") for different architectural scenarios:

| Grant Type | Target Scenario | User Present? | Recommended Today? |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Authorization Code + PKCE** | Web apps, Single-Page Apps (SPAs), and Native Mobile Apps. | Yes | **Yes (Default Standard)** |
| **Client Credentials** | Machine-to-Machine (M2M) communication (e.g., a cron job or microservice calling another internal API). | No | **Yes (For M2M)** |
| **Device Authorization Flow** | Input-constrained devices without browsers (Smart TVs, CLI tools, IoT devices). User logs in on a secondary phone/laptop using a short code. | Yes (Secondary Device) | **Yes (For Smart Devices/CLI)** |
| **Refresh Token Grant** | Silently obtaining a new Access Token after the previous one expires. | No (Background) | **Yes (With Token Rotation)** |
| **Implicit Flow** | Legacy browser apps that returned tokens directly in the URL hash fragment (`#access_token=...`). | Yes | **No (Deprecated — Vulnerable to token leakage)** |
| **Resource Owner Password (ROPC)** | Legacy apps collecting raw username/password directly in their own form and sending them to Auth0. | Yes | **No (Deprecated — Breaks federated SSO & MFA)** |

---

## 7. Essential Auth0 Architectural Concepts

When configuring OAuth 2.0 and OIDC inside **Auth0**, four core configuration entities map directly to the protocol concepts above:

* **Auth0 Tenant:** An isolated logical environment (e.g., `dev-company.us.auth0.com` vs. `prod-company.us.auth0.com`) that acts as the **Authorization Server / OpenID Provider**. Every tenant has its own user store, signing keys, and configurations.
* **Applications (Clients):** Representations of frontends, mobile apps, or M2M services registered inside Auth0. Each Application receives a unique `client_id` (and `client_secret` for confidential apps) and enforces strict allowlists for `Allowed Callback URLs` (`redirect_uri`) and `Allowed Logout URLs`.
* **APIs (Resource Servers):** Representations of backend services registered in Auth0. Each API is assigned a unique **Identifier** (which becomes the `aud` claim in Access Tokens) and defines custom **Permissions (Scopes)** such as `read:analytics` or `manage:billing`.
* **OIDC Discovery Endpoint (`/.well-known/openid-configuration`):** Every Auth0 tenant automatically exposes a public JSON metadata endpoint at `https://<TENANT_DOMAIN>/.well-known/openid-configuration`. Client SDKs and APIs query this single URL to automatically discover the `/authorize` URL, `/oauth/token` URL, `/userinfo` URL, and the `/jwks.json` public signing keys without hardcoding endpoints.

---

## 8. Critical Security Best Practices

* **Never Use an ID Token to Authorize an API:** An ID Token's audience (`aud`) is the Client application, not the backend API. APIs must strictly accept **Access Tokens** validated against the API's specific audience identifier.
* **Always Validate Token Signatures and Claims:** Never trust a decoded JWT payload without verifying its cryptographic signature using Auth0's JWKS keys, and always verify `iss` (issuer), `aud` (audience), and `exp` (expiration).
* **Use Refresh Token Rotation:** In browser-based applications, configure Auth0 to rotate Refresh Tokens on every use. If a stolen Refresh Token is replayed, Auth0 immediately detects reuse and invalidates the entire token family.
* **Enforce Exact `redirect_uri` Matching:** Never use wildcards in callback URLs. Strict URL matching ensures Auth0 never sends an Authorization Code to an attacker-controlled domain.
* **Keep Access Tokens Short-Lived:** Set Access Token lifetimes to short durations (e.g., 5 to 60 minutes) to limit the impact if a token is ever compromised.

notes.title: SentenceTransformers: Vector Database Integration, Benchmarking & Model Selection
notes.content:
# SentenceTransformers: Vector Database Integration 

---

Once a SentenceTransformer converts text into dense embeddings, a **Vector Database** or similarity search index stores, indexes, and retrieves those vectors at millisecond latency across millions or billions of records.

---

## 1. End-to-End Retrieval Architecture

```
[OFFLINE INDEXING PIPELINE]
Documents ──▶ Chunking (256-512 tokens) ──▶ SentenceTransformer.encode() ──▶ [ Vector DB Index ]
                                                                                     ▲
[ONLINE QUERY PIPELINE]                                                              │ ANN Search
User Query ───────────────────────────────▶ SentenceTransformer.encode() ────────────┘
                                                                                     │
Final Answer ◀── LLM / Application ◀── Top-K Docs ◀── Optional CrossEncoder Rerank ◀─┘
```

---

## 2. Exact vs. Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) Search

* **Flat / Exact Search (Brute Force).** Compares the query vector against every single stored vector. Guarantees **100% recall**, but latency degrades linearly (`O(N)`). Practical up to ~50,000–100,000 vectors.
* **HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World).** Builds a multi-layered proximity graph in memory. Enables logarithmic search speed (`O(log N)`) with 95%–99% recall. The industry standard for Qdrant and pgvector.
* **IVF (Inverted File Index).** Clusters vectors into Voronoi cells using K-Means. At query time, only the nearest `nprobe` clusters are searched, trading slight recall for lower RAM usage.
* **Product Quantization (PQ) & Scalar Quantization (SQ).** Compresses 32-bit floats (`float32`) into 8-bit integers (`int8`) or compact centroids, cutting memory footprints by 4x to 32x.

---

## 3. Comparing FAISS, Qdrant, and pgvector

| Feature | FAISS | Qdrant | pgvector |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Architecture** | C++/Python in-memory library | Dedicated Rust vector search engine | PostgreSQL relational extension |
| **Persistence & CRUD** | Manual disk serialization (`write_index`) | Native real-time CRUD, WAL, & snapshots | Full ACID compliance inside Postgres |
| **Metadata Filtering** | Not built-in (requires manual post-filtering) | Pre-filtering integrated directly into HNSW | Full SQL `WHERE` joins and hybrid queries |
| **Index Types** | Flat, HNSW, IVF, PQ, GPU indices | HNSW, Payload indices, Sparse vectors | HNSW, IVFFlat |
| **Quantization** | SQ, PQ, Binary | Scalar (`int8`), Product, Binary | `halfvec` (`float16`), Binary (`bit`) |
| **Best Use Case** | Offline research, batch clustering, GPU search | High-scale production RAG & microservice APIs | Apps already running on PostgreSQL |

---

## 4. Implementation Patterns

### A. FAISS (Local High-Speed Library)
Ensure vectors are L2-normalized (`normalize_embeddings=True`) when using `IndexFlatIP` so Inner Product equals exact Cosine Similarity.

```python
import faiss
import numpy as np
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")
docs = ["Reset password via settings.", "Billing cycles run monthly.", "API keys live in developer tab."]
embeddings = model.encode(docs, normalize_embeddings=True).astype("float32")

# Create Inner Product index (384 dimensions)
dimension = embeddings.shape[1]
index = faiss.IndexFlatIP(dimension)
index.add(embeddings)

# Search top 2 matches
query_vec = model.encode(["Where do I find my API token?"], normalize_embeddings=True).astype("float32")
scores, indices = index.search(query_vec, k=2)

for score, idx in zip(scores[0], indices[0]):
    print(f"Score: {score:.4f} | Doc: {docs[idx]}")
```

### B. Qdrant (Production Vector Engine with Filtering)
Qdrant stores dense vectors alongside JSON payloads, enabling filtered semantic search without losing recall.

```python
from qdrant_client import QdrantClient, models
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")
client = QdrantClient(":memory:")  # Replace with URL for production server

client.create_collection(
    collection_name="knowledge_base",
    vectors_config=models.VectorParams(size=384, distance=models.Distance.COSINE),
)

docs = [
    {"text": "Configure SSO with SAML 2.0.", "tier": "enterprise"},
    {"text": "Export CSV reports from dashboard.", "tier": "free"},
]
vectors = model.encode([d["text"] for d in docs], normalize_embeddings=True)

client.upsert(
    collection_name="knowledge_base",
    points=[
        models.PointStruct(id=i, vector=vectors[i].tolist(), payload=docs[i])
        for i in range(len(docs))
    ],
)

query_vec = model.encode("How do I set up single sign-on?", normalize_embeddings=True).tolist()
hits = client.query_points(
    collection_name="knowledge_base",
    query=query_vec,
    query_filter=models.Filter(
        must=[models.FieldCondition(key="tier", match=models.MatchValue(value="enterprise"))]
    ),
    limit=1,
).points
print("Top Filtered Hit:", hits[0].payload)
```

### C. pgvector (PostgreSQL Extension)
Ideal for transactional applications needing relational joins alongside vector search.

```sql
-- 1. Enable extension and create table
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector;

CREATE TABLE documents (
    id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    content TEXT,
    category TEXT,
    embedding VECTOR(384)
);

-- 2. Build HNSW index for Cosine Distance (<=> operator)
CREATE INDEX ON documents USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops)
WITH (m = 16, ef_construction = 64);

-- 3. Query nearest neighbors with relational filtering
SELECT id, content, 1 - (embedding <=> '[0.012, -0.045, ...]'::vector) AS cosine_similarity
FROM documents
WHERE category = 'security'
ORDER BY embedding <=> '[0.012, -0.045, ...]'::vector
LIMIT 5;
```

---

## 5. Production Pitfalls to Avoid for Vector Database Integration

1. **Metric Mismatch.** Training or normalizing for Cosine Similarity while indexing with Euclidean Distance (`L2`) without unit normalization skews rankings. Always align the index distance metric with the model's training objective.
2. **Missing Task Prefixes.** Asymmetric models (such as `e5` or `bge` variants) require prefixes like `"query: "` at search time and `"passage: "` at indexing time; omitting them degrades retrieval accuracy.
3. **Model Lock-In.** Embeddings from different models occupy incompatible vector spaces. Upgrading from a 384-dim model to a 768-dim model requires re-encoding and re-indexing the entire corpus.

---

# Benchmarking & Model Selection

> Choosing an embedding model solely by its overall average rank on a leaderboard often leads to poor production results. Effective model selection requires matching **domain-specific benchmarks**, **context limits**, and **compute budgets** to the target workload.

## 6. Understanding the MTEB Leaderboard

The **Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB)** evaluates embedding models across dozens of datasets spanning 8 distinct task categories:

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    MTEB LEADERBOARD TASK TAXONOMY                       │
├──────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Task Category        │ Core Metric & Real-World Equivalent              │
├──────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 1. Retrieval         │ NDCG@10  ──▶ RAG, Search Engines, Q&A            │
│ 2. Reranking         │ MAP      ──▶ Ordering candidate search results   │
│ 3. Clustering        │ V-Measure──▶ Topic discovery, ticket grouping    │
│ 4. Pair Classification│ AP      ──▶ Duplicate detection, paraphrase     │
│ 5. Classification    │ Accuracy ──▶ Sentiment, intent routing           │
│ 6. STS (Similarity)  │ Spearman ──▶ Semantic text comparison            │
│ 7. Summarization     │ Spearman ──▶ Evaluating summary quality          │
│ 8. Bitext Mining     │ F1       ──▶ Cross-lingual translation matching  │
└──────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### How to Read MTEB Columns Correctly
1. **Filter by Task First.** For a RAG pipeline or search engine, ignore the overall MTEB average and sort strictly by the **Retrieval (`NDCG@10`)** column. A model that excels at Classification may perform poorly at Retrieval.
2. **Check Domain Sub-Benchmarks.** Modern MTEB includes specialized domain splits—such as **MTEB Legal**, **MTEB Finance**, **MTEB Medical**, and **MTEB Code**. Always prioritize domain-specific scores over generic Wikipedia/web averages.
3. **Inspect Model Size & Memory (VRAM).** Top leaderboard spots are often held by 7B-parameter LLM embedders requiring 14+ GB of VRAM. Compare parameter counts against latency SLAs; a 110M–330M parameter model often delivers 95% of the retrieval accuracy at 10x the speed.
4. **Verify Max Tokens & Embedding Dimensions.** Confirm that `Max Tokens` fits the chunking strategy and `Embedding Dimensions` fits RAM/storage budgets (or supports Matryoshka truncation).

---

## 7. Step-by-Step Model Selection Decision Tree

```
START: What is the primary task?
  │
  ├──▶ Short Query searching Long Documents (RAG / Search)?
  │      ├── Need < 10ms CPU latency & low RAM? ──▶ all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (384d) or BGE-small
  │      ├── Need Long Context (up to 8192 tokens)? ──▶ BAAI/bge-m3 or nomic-embed-text
  │      └── Need Maximum Accuracy (GPU available)? ──▶ Top Retrieval MTEB model + CrossEncoder Reranker
  │
  ├──▶ Comparing Similar-Length Texts (Clustering / Deduplication)?
  │      └── Sort MTEB by Clustering (V-Measure) & STS ──▶ all-mpnet-base-v2 or GTE-base
  │
  └──▶ Multi-Language or Cross-Lingual Search?
         └── Filter MTEB by target language ──▶ BAAI/bge-m3 or multilingual-e5-large
```

---

## 8. Running Custom Domain Benchmarks

Public leaderboards suffer from potential **data contamination** (models inadvertently seeing benchmark test sets during pre-training). Always validate candidate models on a small, private **Golden Dataset** (100–500 real domain queries paired with ground-truth relevant documents).

### Key Evaluation Metrics
* **Recall@K.** Percentage of queries where the true relevant document appears within the top `K` retrieved results (e.g., `Recall@5`, `Recall@20`). Crucial for ensuring the LLM in a RAG system receives the right context.
* **MRR@K (Mean Reciprocal Rank).** Rewards placing the *first* correct answer at rank #1 (`1/1 = 1.0`) versus rank #2 (`1/2 = 0.5`).
* **NDCG@K (Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain).** The standard MTEB retrieval metric; evaluates both relevance and rank position when multiple documents are relevant.

---

## 9. Automated Evaluation Code with `InformationRetrievalEvaluator`

SentenceTransformers includes built-in evaluators to benchmark any candidate model on custom domain data in seconds:

```python
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
from sentence_transformers.evaluation import InformationRetrievalEvaluator

# 1. Define private domain queries, corpus, and ground-truth mappings
queries = {
    "q1": "What causes an OOMKilled error in Kubernetes?",
    "q2": "How to configure TLS certificates on an ingress controller?",
}

corpus = {
    "doc1": "Pods exceeding their memory limit are terminated by the kernel with exit code 137 (OOMKilled).",
    "doc2": "Horizontal Pod Autoscalers scale replicas based on CPU or custom metrics.",
    "doc3": "Ingress TLS is configured by referencing a Kubernetes Secret containing tls.crt and tls.key.",
}

relevant_docs = {
    "q1": {"doc1"},
    "q2": {"doc3"},
}

# 2. Initialize the evaluator
ir_evaluator = InformationRetrievalEvaluator(
    queries=queries,
    corpus=corpus,
    relevant_docs=relevant_docs,
    name="k8s-domain-eval",
    ndcg_at_k=[10],
    mrr_at_k=[10],
    accuracy_at_k=[1, 3],
)

# 3. Compare multiple candidate models
candidates = ["all-MiniLM-L6-v2", "BAAI/bge-base-en-v1.5"]

for model_name in candidates:
    model = SentenceTransformer(model_name)
    results = ir_evaluator(model)
    print(f"=== {model_name} ===")
    print(f"NDCG@10:   {results['k8s-domain-eval_cosine_ndcg@10']:.4f}")
    print(f"MRR@10:    {results['k8s-domain-eval_cosine_mrr@10']:.4f}")
    print(f"Recall@1:  {results['k8s-domain-eval_cosine_accuracy@1']:.4f}
")
```
