If the frame reaches right most corners in the input matrix, then we need to move the frame one or more than one step below from left most corner. This process is called sliding. Suppose, our kernel is a 3 × 3 matrix. So, from our input matrix (Figure 6.3), we have to choose a 3 × 3 matrix as receptive field.

![](assets/figure-02-f0f4c1540e0453c1a83e3ca4.png)

Figure 6.3: Receptive field selection (Adapted from [7])

Here, our receptive field is  and chosen kernel is .

We will keep iterating the convolution equation from i = |m| = 2, j = |n| = 2 to i, j = 0. Initially, m, n = 0 and after each of the iteration we need to increment m, n by 1.

Our computed value  = () + () + () + () + … + ()

Now we keep sliding and computing, p 2', p 3'… in the same way we computed p 1'. Notice that after performing convolution operation on a 4 × 4 input matrix, the output is a 2 × 2 matrix. This 2 × 2 output matrix is known as feature map.

A series of convolution operations are performed in a convolutional layer. A convolutional layer performs three major tasks: convolution, max pooling, fully connected neural network operation. Convolution and max pooling operations perform multiple times. The final output of convolution and max pooling operations is the input for neural network. By performing convolution and max pooling multiple times, we can flatten the feature map that is a multi-dimensional matrix, into a fixed size multi-dimensional matrix [4]. A shared neural network is required a fixed length input for both training and prediction process. The following diagram shows a convolutional layer architecture called VGG16 [5].

![](assets/figure-03-2a470534d87ccdf10d3eb42f.png)

Figure 3.3: VGG16 convolutional network architecture (Adapted from [8])

The above figure contains six convolution layer and one neural network layer. As an input image passes more convolutional layer, the height and width of feature map decrease and depth increases. Based on the previous layer information, each convolutional layer creates abstractions. The first convolutional layer generally learns edges in the input images, the second convolutional layer searches for pattern in edges, and so on. In the final convolutional layer, it generates a much smaller dimensional feature map with greater depth (7×7×512). 

The max pooling operation decreases the height and width of the feature map and the depth increases depending on the total number of filters used by a convolutional network.

**3.1. MAX POOLING:**

Max pooling selects the maximum value of all selected squares to make feature detection more robust. Figure 6.6 shows the max pooling process. It reduces the spatial dimension (w × h) of the input volume for the next convolution layer. Max pooling does not affect the depth dimension of the input data. It is also known as down-sampling. The reason behind using max pooling is it finds out the most relevant parts of the images. If we think the values in a matrix as the pixel intensity, then by selecting the height intensity, we are going to get a feature that is most relevant [6]. If we do not perform convolution operation and max pooling in convolution layer, then neural network layer has to connect a lot of neurons (pixel values) from one layer to another layer. Connecting every single pixel value in an image to every single pixel value in the next layer is very much costly and time consume.

![](assets/figure-04-8e24f0b27d933de9e2fba51a.png)

Figure 6.6: Max pooling operation (Adapted from [7])

In figure 6.6, we have divided a 4 × 4 matrix into four 2 × 2 matrices and then constructed a new 2 × 2 matrix selecting the maximum pixel value from each of 2 × 2 matrices. We need to keep in mind that we have to divide a matrix into smaller square matrices (e.g., 2 × 2 or 3 × 3). Otherwise, when multiple pixel values in a divided square matrix, which is comparatively large (e.g., 10 × 10), are large numbers, selecting the maximum number can cause feature loss. When we lose one or more intense pixels from an input matrix, we call it feature loss.

**4. INSTANCE SEGMENTATION:**

Mask Region-based Convolutional Neural Network (Mask RCNN) works toward the problem of instance segmentation [1]. Instance segmentation is a combination of two sub-problems. The first one is object detection. This is the problem of finding and classifying a variable number of objects in an image. They are variable numbers because the number of objects detected in an image can vary from image to image. The second part of instance segmentation is semantic segmentation. Semantic segmentation is the understanding of an image at the pixel level assigning an object class to each pixel of target objects.

![](assets/figure-05-e2d34ce7f1a69018d528500b.png)

Figure 4.1: Segmented image (Source. [1])

Using object detection and semantic segmentation together, we get instance segmentation [1]. In the above image, the rectangular bounding boxes are created from object detection and the shaded masks are output of semantic segmentation.

Now that we have a high-level intuition of instance segmentation, we will take a look at the architecture behind Mask RCNN. Since there are two phases, we have two parts. For object detection, we use Faster RCNN algorithm and for semantic segmentation, we use Fully Connected Network (FCN). So, the architecture of Mask RCNN is basically the combination of Faster RCNN and FCN architecture [1]. 

![](assets/figure-06-99f7e2b6b31467510b981d6b.png)

Figure 4.2: Overall Mask RCNN process (Source. [1])

Figure 4.2 shows overall Mask RCNN process. First of all, Faster RCNN takes an input image and passes the image through a convolutional layer. The output of this layer is a multi-dimensional matrix of pixels with identified object region, also known as Region of Interest (RoI). An algorithm called RoI pooling is used to pull a region. The pulled region is passed through a neural network layer that performs classification task for object detection and bounding box regression task to identify object location in the image. Secondly, for semantic segmentation, the pulled region is passed through another convolutional layer. In this layer, each of the pixels goes through a neural network. The neural network classifies whether a pixel is responsible for constructing a target object. we will explain the details process of training Mask RCNN, object detection using Faster RCNN and semantic segmentation by using fully connected neural network (FCN) in this report.

**4.1. TRAINING A MASK RCNN MODEL:**

For training Mask RCNN model, we need to provide annotated image as training dataset. The following diagram shows the overall training process.

![](assets/figure-07-d9fa0b6d166bd154238898ff.png)

Figure 4.3: Mask RCNN training process (Adapted from [2])

First of all, we are going to pass a training image through convolutional layer. For explaining the training process, we have used here VGG16 convolutional layer that has explained in section 3. In Figure 3.3 (VGG16 convolutional architecture), 5th convolution layer generates a feature map that has 512 pixel depth. The feature map contains our annotated RoI. An algorithm called RoI pooling slides a window through the entire feature map and extract annotated RoI which is a 7×7×512 dimensional feature map. All of the pixels in this RoI connect to a neural network.

While training a neural network, the primary task is to find the optimal numeric value for weights and biases for each data row (in our case, each pixel). The weight and bias are neural network parameters. The optimal values of weights and biases for a pixel generate an output that is equal to the ground truth. Let’s consider the following neural network where the first layer, also known as input layer, contains all of the pixels from 7×7×512-d feature map.

![](assets/figure-08-8964482929001261e3ff20fd.png)

Figure 4.4: Sample neural network for Mask RCNN training (Adapted from [6])

For simplicity, let’s consider training x1 pixel using two hidden layers and a final output layer. First of all, we need to propagate forward through the network. While we propagate forward through a neural network, each neuron computes a prediction value for each pixel [6]. In final output layer, we get prediction values that describe whether x1 pixel belongs to balloon image. The final layer provides output as object (range 0 to 1) or not-object (range 0 to 1). Initially, we need to choose a ground truth threshold value and random weight and bias value. After propagating forward, in final output layer, if the difference between neural network prediction and ground truth threshold is greater than 0, we apply the back-propagation algorithm. In back-propagation, first, we propagate one step backward (H2) and update weights and bias using gradient descent algorithm [7]. To update weights and bias, first, we compute loss for weights and bias in H2. Then, we reduce the computed loss from previous weights and bias values. Once the weights and bias in H2 are updated, we propagate one step backward (H1). The back-propagation process keeps running until it reaches in the input layer. When the back-propagation algorithm reaches at the input layer, the neural network starts forward propagation again. This process keeps running until the difference between the neural network prediction and ground truth threshold value is 0 or approximately 0. At the end of the training process, neural network stores the optimal weights and biases values. These values are used to make inference on new input.

**4.2. FASTER RCNN:**

Faster RCNN is an approach to bounding box object detection [2]. It performs object detection in two stages. First, it determines single or multiple Regions of Interest (RoI) going through the feature map. This is done using the RPN (Regions Proposal Network) algorithm. RPN finds out all possible object regions or RoI in an image. Secondly, for each RoI, we determine the class label (target object or not-target object) using neural network.

In Faster RCNN, we first take our input image and compute a convolutional feature map passing the image through a convolutional network layer. Feature map is outcome of convolutional operation between matrix of pixel value and kernel matrix [7]. After that, RPN process works on the feature map. The RPN module looks directly at the convolutional feature map and is able to produce Region Proposals or RoI directly from that convolutional feature map. In other words, the RPN module informs Faster RCNN about regions in the image on which the detection process will work [1]. Figure 4.5 shows overall Faster RCNN process.

![](assets/figure-09-23a53a7018f0a9a86f49d022.png)

Figure 4.5: Overall Faster RCNN architecture (Adapted from [2])

In Faster RCNN, a test input image is provided to the convolutional layer. In 4th convolutional layer, VGG16 creates 28×28×512-d feature map and in 5th convolutional layer, VGG16 creates 14×14×512-d feature map. We need to apply RPN algorithm on any of the feature map. The RPN algorithm then finds out all possible objects (regions proposal or RoI) going through the feature map in 4th or 5th layer. An algorithm called RoI pooling extracts all of the identified RoI following the sliding window approach [2]. Each RoI participates in a fully connected neural network. The neural network works with every pixel of a RoI to classify whether a RoI belongs to a target object, for example, balloon object. In the final layer, a neural network provides output as object or not-object with a probability (0-1). After a neural network classifies the RoI of target balloon object, another algorithm called bounding box regression starts working on RoI of balloon object. The task of bounding box regression is to find out the location of balloon object in an input image. Feature map contains pixel values and pixel coordinates information. Using pixel coordinate information, bounding box regression algorithm provides x,y-coordinates value, height, and width as output.

**4.3. REGION PROPOSAL NETWORK (RPN):**

RPN is an algorithm for detecting all possible objects in an image and for helping to identify bounding box location for target object [1]. A bounding box is a rectangular box that surrounds a particular object in an image. In RPN, we follow n × n sliding window approach over our convolutional feature map [1]. The sliding window approach is also considered as a convolutional operation. Position of the sliding window relative to the feature map tells us where we are in the image and bounding box regression provides final localization information with reference to this sliding window [1]. The bounding box regression uses the notion of different anchor boxes. Anchor boxes are rectangular regions in a sliding window that tell us whether our target object or part of our target object is present in a sliding window. While we slide a n × n window over a feature map, the RPN predicts single or multiple region proposals or RoI. RPN detects BLOB (Binary Large Object) like object in an image. BLOB can be defined as a group of connected pixels in a binary image. After performing convolution operations using multiple filters (for example, edge detection filter), objects get highlighted and their pixels get connected.

The following diagram shows a convolutional output after applying edge detection convolution operation. In a convoluted feature map (multi-dimensional matrix) the object pixels are connected. By connected, it means that there is a similarity among the pixels of an object in convoluted feature map. Edge detection filter highlights object edges in an image showed in Figure 4.6. All the pixels inside the balloon edge are considered as balloon pixels and these pixels are connected. RPN finds out such pixels in an image and detects objects.

![](assets/figure-10-1b8d3db39884eaa401508ac5.png)

Figure 4.6: Generated feature map after applying edge detection filter

**4.3.1 ANCHORS:**

In the following example, we have showed how anchors are generated and how generated anchors are used to generate 7×7×512 feature map in 6th layer of VGG16 convolutional network architecture.

![](assets/figure-11-708fbb0897e8484b0363bf62.png)

Figure 4.3.1: Anchor processing (Adapted from [2])

Let’s consider the above image as an input image from test dataset. Faster RCNN accepts any size image as input. But before generating feature map from that image, Faster RCNN converts the image into 600 pixel (height, H) height and corresponding scaled width, for example 1000 (width, W) pixel. When we resize an image maintaining scale or aspect ratio, we only have to provide either height or width value. The corresponding scaled size will be computed based on our provided height or width value (600 pixel). 

Blue rectangular regions are our RoI detected by RPN. The red rectangular box is one of the anchors that generate from a particular sliding window position. The overlap part between an anchor and one of our RoI is called Intersection over Union (IoU).

IoU = 

Here, A denotes an anchor and GT denotes ground truth. Anchor holds information whether an overlapped area contains target object or not. We can identify whether an anchor contains target object or not by using IoU value. If IoU value > 0.7, then an anchor is considered as a part of an object. On the other hand, if IoU value < 0.3, then an anchor is considered as a part of a not-object [1]. If all computed IoU value < 0.7, the algorithm will choose anchors that have maximum IoU value.

When we pass our input image through a convolutional architecture (VGG16), in 4th convolution layer, VGG16 generates a feature map with depth 512 pixels. Now we move a 3×3 sliding window through the entire feature map. The sliding window steps forward by one pixel at a time. For a sliding window with 3 scales and 3 aspect ratio, k = 9 anchor are generated in each sliding window position [2]. An entire feature map with height H and width W contains HWk number of total anchors where k is total generated anchors in each sliding window position (k = 9). The generated 9 anchors in each sliding window have three different scale (128, 256, and 512) and three different ratios (1:1, 1:2, and 2:1) [2].

![](assets/figure-12-28bb3fc66952556452ed9872.png)

Figure 4.3.2: Nine types of anchors (Adapted from [1])

So, total generated anchors for a 28×28 dimensional feature map in 4th layer of VGG16 architecture are 28×28×9 = 6300 for all sliding window position through the entire feature map. Total generated anchors (6300) contain a lot of unnecessary anchors. To remove the unnecessary anchors, first of all, we ignore cross-boundary anchors shown in the above image (red rectangular anchor). After ignoring cross-boundary anchors, total number of anchors get reduced by one third. 

![](assets/figure-13-bda9bfe25696bc460655c5a5.png)

Figure 4.3.3: Cross-boundary anchors (Adapted from [2])

Secondly, we apply Non-Max Suppression (NMS) technique. The bellow diagram shows NMS process. The blue box here is a detected object region by RPN, red and green boxes are two anchors. The two anchors have a large overlap area (IoU value >= 0.7) inside the ground truth box. The idea is we choose such anchors that have large IoU value from the remaining anchors after ignoring cross-boundary anchors [2]. After applying NMS technique on remaining anchors, total number of anchors again get reduced by one third.

![](assets/figure-14-6744032d77dc91aa36b4a96a.png)

Figure 4.3.4: NMS Technique (Adapted from [2])

In VGG16 convolutional architecture, a 512 dimensional matrix is generated for each RoI aggregating several anchors that have large IoU values. This 512-d matrix is sent to a neural network layer. The neural network layer performs two major tasks. Firstly, a binary classifier classifies whether it’s an object or not object. This classification process is occurred in pixel level. For each node (pixel value) it will output a probability between 0 and 1. Secondly, another algorithm called bounding box regression works on the classified RoI for target object. Bounding-box regression identify x-y coordinates, height, and weight of an object to draw a rectangular box surrounding object region.

While neural networks classify an object pixel by pixel, it outputs a numeric value (between 0 and 1) for every pixel in final output layer. A numeric value shows the probability of a pixel’s belonging to an object. Final output layer also contains activation functions that convert probability value to positive or negative (object or not-object) depending on a threshold value. To compute the final score or confidence value that shows on top of a rectangular box, we compute sum of all positive pixels probability values and find the average.

**4.4. SEMANTIC SEGMENTATION:**

Mask RCNN uses Fully Connected Network (FCN) for semantic segmentation [1]. FCN works based on dense prediction that is pixel wise class labeling. 

We already know that in 5th convolutional layer, Faster RCNN runs a sliding window and for each RoI, it generates a 512-d matrix that goes through a neural network for classification and then another algorithm called bounding box regression identifies object location in the input image [1]. For semantic segmentation, a fully connected neural network takes all pixel values from target RoI matrix as input. The neural network performs classification task for each pixel identifying object pixel or not-object pixel comparing between neural network prediction and a defined threshold value.

![](assets/figure-15-ed6e1b5a23338617990de6ba.png)

Figure 4.4.1: Pixel segmentation process (Adapted from [1])

While making inference on a new image, the neural network uses stored weights to classify whether a pixel is a part of target object. If a pixel is classified as a part of a target object, a binary mask 1 gets added on top of the pixel, shown in Figure 4.4.1. Otherwise, a binary mask 0 gets added on top of the pixel. We then find out the pixels that have binary mask 1 and add color splash.

**5. EXPERIMENTS AND RESULTS:**

In this section, first of all, we will test effect of two different models trained on two different choice of training dataset. And then we will compare our trained model with an existing model trained by the vendor of Mask RCNN algorithm.

To train our Mask RCNN segmentation models, we have used balloon dataset. First, we have trained a model using 60 training images. At the end of each epoch, we save the optimal weights and biases in a file. Secondly, we have trained another model randomly picking 40 images out of 60. The optimal weights and biases for this training have been saved into a separate file. We have compared the output of these two models using a common test dataset that contains 13 test images. The differences are observed in instance segmentation and confidence score. The following diagram shows the difference in instance segmentation.

![](assets/figure-16-13246dccdeb34d4a07135767.png)

Figure 5.1: Comparison between our two trained models

In Figure 5.1, the first image is the output of the model that has been trained using 60 balloon images and the second image is the output of the model that has been trained using 40 random balloon images. In second image, pixel wise masking is missing in almost half of the balloon area whereas pixel wise masking covers more area in first image.

For some balloon object, the confidence score in the output images of first model is higher than the confidence score in the output images of second model. The following table shows the differences in confidence score between two models for some test images. Model 1 and Model 2 columns contain confidence for each detected balloon object.

Table 1: Confidence score of two trained models

| Total balloon object | Has balloon overlap | Model-1 score | Model-2 score |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 3 | No | 0.98, 0.96, 0.98 | 0.94, 0.96, 0.95 |
| 2 | No | 0.99, 1.00 | 0.99, 0.97 |
| 4 | Yes | 0.96, 0.98, 0.94, 0.98 | 0.92, 0.98, 0.91, 0.92 |
The differences in confidence scores have been observed in three types of test images- first, the image that contain multiple balloon objects without any overlap of balloons and second, the image that contains multiple balloon objects with overlaps of balloons. The above table shows that for these three types of test image, model-1 provides higher confidence score than model-2.

A Mask RCNN segmentation model has already been trained by the vendor of the algorithm using the balloon dataset. We have used their trained weights and biases and our test dataset to output segmented images. In Figure 5.2, the first image is an output of our trained model and the second image is an output of the existing model.

![](assets/figure-17-1730fa062e931daad8e0c7b5.png)

Figure 5.2: Comparison between our trained mode and existing trained model

We found the major difference in the above diagram where our trained model predicts a helmet as a balloon in the right output image. Beside this difference, for several images, the confidence score is higher in existing trained model than our trained model and existing segmentation model draw segmentation mask more preciously.

**6. CONCLUSION:**

In conclusion, we can improve segmentation and confidence score by training our model more robustly using a lower learning rate and also trying different neural network settings. A neural network setting contains total number of layers in a neural network and total number of neurons in a hidden layer. In our project, we have used a learning rate 0.01 to train our model whereas the existing mode trained by the algorithm vendor has used a learning rate 0.001. Our training process takes longer time to train our segmentation model. The future study of our project is to improve training time by allowing parallel data processing using GPU.

**REFERENCES:**

1. Kaiming He, Georgia Gkioxari, Piotr Dollar, Ross Girshick, "Mask R-CNN", arXiv:1703.06870v3 [cs.CV] 24 Jan 2018.

2. Shaoqing Ren, Kaiming He, Ross Girshick, Jian Sun, "Faster R-CNN: Towards Real-Time Object Detection with Region Proposal Networks", arXiv: 1505.05836, 2015.

3. Yuhua Chen, Wen Li, Christos Sakaridis, Dengxin Dai, Luc Van, Gool, "Domain Adaptive Faster R-CNN for Object Detection in the Wild".

4. Ross Girshick, "Fast R-CNN", arXiv:1504.08083v2 [cs.CV] 27 Sep 2015.

5. Karen Simonyan, Andrew Zisserman, "VERY DEEP CONVOLUTIONAL NETWORKS FOR LARGE-SCALE IMAGE RECOGNITION", arXiv:1409.1556v6 [cs.CV] 10 Apr 2015.

6. Michael Nielsen, “CHAPTER 6: Deep Learning”, Url: www.neuralnetworksanddeeplearning.com/chap6.html (online book)

7. Ian Goodfellow, Yoshua Bengio, Aaron Courville, "Deep Learning Book", Published- November 18, 2016.

8. Xiangyu Zhang, Jianhua Zou, Kaiming He, Jian Sun, "Accelerating Very Deep Convolutional Networks for Classification and Detection", arXiv:1505.06798v2 [cs.CV] 18 Nov 2015.

9. Tensorflow Documentation ([www.tensorflow.org/api_docs/python/](https://www.tensorflow.org/api_docs/python/))

notes.content:
**ABSTRACT:**

In classification problem of supervised learning, presence of imbalanced classes in a dataset is quite a common issue. Before classifying an imbalanced dataset, it is necessary to oversample the minority classes. As the oversampling technique generates synthetic data points closer to the minority classes, there is a possibility that the generated classification model might provide a biased prediction toward minority oversampled dataset that causes overfitting issue while we provide new data points after training a model. In this report, we have conducted a details study on different imbalanced datasets that contain different number of observations to find out the overfitting issue with oversampling technique. After identifying the scenario of the generated overfitting issue, we have applied a different oversampling algorithm to solve the overfitting issue. The major task of this project is to figure out the situation when the overfitting issue arises.

**1. INTRODUCTION:**

Imbalanced dataset defines a problem in which case the number of classes are not equal. By not equal, it typically means that the number of majority classes are far from the number of minority classes. There is an accuracy paradox related to the imbalanced dataset. According to accuracy paradox, after classifying an imbalanced dataset, we might achieve a 99 percent of model accuracy, but while we provide new data to that model for prediction, it predicts very poorly.

Through our project, we have used Linear SVM classifier to classify our multiple dataset that contain variable number of observations. We will provide intuition about SVM classifier cost function and few other terms that are relevant while we are explaining an imbalanced class problem before diving into details in the next sections. For predictive data modeling, our chosen dataset contains two major data part. The first one is features and the second one is class labels. In a dataset, features are the independent variables based on which data we generate a predictive modeling. On the other hand, a class label is a provided output in a dataset for a particular set of features. Each of the data row in a dataset is known as observation. We are going to use these three terms frequently through our report.

For evaluating Linear SVM classification model, we have used accuracy, precision, and recall value. In a predictive modeling, accuracy shows the ratio of total true predictions and total number of observations. We can obtain recall value dividing true positive prediction by total number of actual positive prediction. And we can obtain precision value dividing total true positive prediction by total number of predicted positive observations. We have discussed more about precision and recall in evaluation measures section.

For oversampling, classifying, and showing classification details, we have used python throughout the project. All the used packages in our project have been managed using anaconda. We have used numpy library for large numerical array computation, matplotlib for plotting data graph, sklearn for applying Linear SVM, imblearn, which is a library for imbalance learn, to apply oversampling technique. We have also used pipeline method from sklearn api. The pipeline method basically manages the sequence of operation. For example, in our oversampling and Linear SVM implementation, we have maintained a sequence by oversampling our imbalanced dataset first, then applying Linear SVM classification algorithm, and finally displaying the classification results.

**2. PROBLEM STATEMENT AND PROJECT GOAL:**

In imbalanced dataset, there is presence of one or more minority class labels and majority class labels. The traditional procedures of classifying such imbalanced dataset provide biased predictions toward the majority class in most of the cases. In order to overcome this problem, we need to oversample or undersample our dataset. In this project, we are going to apply oversampling technique first and then classify the oversampled data.

When we apply oversampling on minority class labels, total number of minority class labels get increased adding synthetic data point similar to the minority class labels. After applying this approach, the number of majority class and the number of minority class become equal. Due to this reason, there is a higher probability of arising overfitting issue in case of minority class labels. This overfitting issue arises depending on the size of provided dataset. Through this report, we will investigate the overfitting issue with minority class oversampling using an oversampling algorithm called SMOTE (Synthetic Minority Over-Sampling) and different size dataset. There is no specific solution to solve this overfitting issue. In this report, we will show that another oversampling algorithm called Borderline SMOTE can be used to solve this overfitting issue. Such comparison study did not take place yet for oversampled minority class of imbalanced dataset.

**3. EXPLANATION OF OVERSAMPLING ALGORITHMS:**

**Synthetic Minority Over-Sampling (SMOTE):**

While we are dealing with the classification problem, the percentage of the classes in the total sample plays an important role. However, there are scenarios where we might be dealing with an imbalanced dataset. By imbalanced we mean there is presence of a minority class.

For example, if we are trying to identify the fraudulent transactions from a dataset, we won’t have them in sufficient numbers. Any stable system will not have five or even ten percent frauds. We may barely have 0.5% or a smaller number of frauds in terms of percentage. In such cases, our model may try to fit the majority class and may provide a biased prediction. At the same time, it gives us a false sense of accuracy. Now in this case, even if we classify all transactions as non-fraudulent, we are going to be 99.5% accurate, but that is not our objective and our model does not help despite giving a very highly accurate result. Some other examples could be that of manufacturing defects with the implementation of **six sigma and** **lim** **practices**. The occurrences of defects have also been reduced greatly. Similarly, if we need to identify rare diseases, natural disaster or even enrollment to premier institutes which have got very low percentage of acceptance compared to the applications they received. Again, we are going to deal with the imbalanced dataset.

One of the ways to deal with such scenarios is to resample the dataset by either decreasing the majority class or by increasing the minority class observations. We can also do that randomly. So, in case of random undersampling, we simply select a small subset of the majority class and keep the minority class as it is. Let’s say we have a dataset of total 1000 observations and 10 observations or 0.1% of those observations are fraud. We may decide to choose only 90 normal observations in this case that will make the fraudulent transactions as 10 % of the total sample size that we have. Definitely, it helps us to balance the dataset. However, it is possible that discarded observations could have some valuable information and such an approach could lead to bias. Similarly, in case of random oversampling, we randomly add more minority observations by copying some or all of those observations on replicating them multiple times. For instance, we may increase the fraudulent transactions from 10 to 110. After this increment, they become 10% of the total observations. So, there is absolutely no information loss as in case of undersampling. However, it is very much prone to overfitting as we have simply copied some observations. That is where the Synthetic Minority Over-Sampling (SMOTE) technique helps us. It creates new synthetic observations or new data point.

First of all, suppose that every data point is plotted. It then identifies the feature vector and its nearest neighbor. After that, it takes the difference between the two. Finally, simply multiply the difference with random between 0 and 1. The next step is to identify a new point on the line segment by adding the random number to the feature vector and then repeat the process for identified feature vectors. The Euclidean between two vectors a and b is given by the following equation.

![](assets/figure-01-f48ba224206f0998d45fda4d.png)

As the first step, we have the data point plotted in two dimensions. The data points inside the rectangular shape are the minority class observations. The right side diagram shows the minority class observation in two dimensional space.

![](assets/figure-02-835bd41d7ca5bd2970fee086.png)

Figure:

Now we are going to identify the feature vectors and its nearest neighbors. In the next step, we calculate the linear distance between p1 and p2 of feature vectors and multiply it by a random number between 0 and 1. We then plot a new data point on the line p1p2 with the result we got. Suppose, the new data point is s1. The feature vector for this new point s1 is our synthetic data point. We continue this computation for all the points and keep on adding synthetic observation on the other lines (shown in the diagram) depending upon how many data points we asked SMOTE to create. By following this approach, from these five points, shown in the diagram, we have created nine new but synthetic observations. Thus, the SMOTE algorithm creates new sample observations when we are dealing with an imbalanced dataset. The formula for generating synthetic data using SMOTE algorithm is given bellow [].

![](assets/figure-03-4667e708157a8287d813f924.png)

Dnew = generated synthetic data point, Di = minority class label in the dataset, Di(hat) = one of the nearest data points from Di, lambda = randomly generated number between 0 and 1.

![](assets/figure-04-775e4f541dfe7ffbabc52b0c.png)

Figure: 

**4.** **EVALUATION MEASURES:**

In most of the case, evaluation measurement for two imbalanced class problems is developed using confusion matrix (Table 1). A confusion matrix is a tabular formatted data that is used to explain the performance as well as the accuracy of a classified model of any specific classification algorithm. It contains total number of correct and incorrect predictions that help to visualize the model accuracy.

<confusion matrix table>

The first row and the first column in the above table represent the actual class and the predicted class label sequentially. Here TP and TN stand for True Positive and True Negative. Similarly, FP and FN stand for False Positive and False Negative. We can calculate the model accuracy dividing the sum of True Positive and True Negative by the total number from the above table.

Accuracy = <eq>

In case of imbalanced class, model accuracy of a particular classification algorithm is not sufficient enough to measure standard performance of that classification model. In order to evaluate the imbalanced class problem, it is necessary to use *Precision*, *Recall*, and *F-value* along with the model accuracy.

Recall is a measurement that illustrates that how many true positive predictions are called among the sum of true positive and false negative predictions. We can compute the recall value of a classification model by dividing the true positive value by the sum of true positive and false negative. In order to calculate precision, we need to divide total positive by the sum of total positive and false positive.

Precision = <eq>

Recall = <eq>

F-value = <eq>

In the above F-val equation, Beta (element of [0, infinity)) is the relational variable between precision and recall. In most of the case, 1 is used as the usual value of beta. When the value of beta is 0, the above equation totally emphasis on the value of recall. On the other hand, when the value of beta is inf, the above equation emphasis on the value of precision.

**5. BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF LINEAR SVM** **CLASSIFICATION:**

Support Vector Machine (SVM) classification is a supervised learning algorithm. SVM is able to perform both classification and regression task. For a classification task, in SVM, we plot each data point in n dimensional space. Here n denotes number of features in our dataset. When we perform a classification task using SVM, it basically finds the plotted hyper plane that demonstrates and separates our data point.

![](assets/figure-05-25f2feba2f64765e78c1f341.png)

Figure: SVM classification sample

In the above figure, three hyperplanes H1, H2, and H3 are generated that separate the plotted data point. After plotting our data point, multiple hyperplane can be generated as separator of different class. In such case, the SVM model selects the appropriate hyperplane that separates the plotted data point in a better way.

**6.** **BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF OVERALL PROCESS:**

In this section, we will go through the summary of entire experimental details from data over-sampling to applying classification algorithm and fixing model overfitting issue if any arises due to the over-sampling process. We choose a toy dataset. The dataset is a feature of Scikit learn api. The reason we choose this dataset is that we can generate data on demand. For our experiment, we need a wide range (small as well as large dataset) of multiple dataset. By using Scikit learn, we can generate various length dataset providing few built in parameter, for example, number of features, number of imbalanced class, number of generated row, weights, and so on. Figure shows the entire process of identifying the overfitting issue and it’s solution.

![](assets/figure-06-fd9d224e824955ce04a7fb47.png)

Figure: Process details

First of all, we are going to generate our dataset. Secondly, we need to pre-process out data. The generated dataset contains categorical data. We need to handle categorical data for both features and class labels. After handling categorical data, we need to apply feature extraction process and training-test dataset split. Thirdly, once data pre-processing is done, as our chosen dataset contains imbalanced class, first, we are going to apply SMOTE algorithm in order to over-sample the dataset. We will visualize out oversampled data using visualization graph. In fourth step, we will apply linear SVM as our classification algorithm. Linear SVM shows the details classification information (confusion matrix, precision, recall). We will analyze the classification details to identify the overfitting issue for a particular dataset.

**7.** **DATA PRE-PROCESSING:**

The entire process of our data preprocessing contains four steps: Feature Scaling, Categorical Data Processing, Process Missing Values, and Training and Test set Split. The following diagram shows the entire process.

![](assets/figure-07-63756c008853f99911920bb9.jpg)

Figure: Data preprocessing steps

First, we are going to apply feature scaling process on our dataset. Feature scaling is the process of standardizing both dependent and independent variables in our dataset. Features in a dataset are known as independent variables and class labels are known as dependent variables. It is quite normal that the range of values of different dependent and independent variables varies widely. Such type of variation causes major problem while we classify our data. Following the feature scaling process, we can overcome this issue. We are going to apply mean normalization on our dataset. The formula for mean normalization is:

![](assets/figure-08-ec44866bc5d2505034b15329.png)

Here, x denotes an original value of a variable and x’ denotes normalized value.

While Scikit learn generates dataset on demand, the generated dataset contains categorical data in features (independent variables). As a machine learning model can process only numerical value, it is necessary to process the categorical features in our dataset. While we process categorical data, each of the categories gets separated into separate column with 0 (false) or 1 (true) value.

We will process missing values computing the mean of all values in a specific column. Finally, we need to split our entire dataset into test and training set. As we are going to use multiple dataset with different data volume, we will split our dataset 25% as test set and rest 75% as training set.

**8.** **EXPERIMENTS:**

After preprocessing our data, we applied SMOTE oversampling technique first and then classify oversampled data using Linear SVM. Data oversampling has been visualized using plotted data graph. For better understanding the provided dataset before and after oversampling, we have generated both plotted diagrams showing scenario of before and after oversampling. In our first experiment, we have worked with a dataset that contains 2500 observations. The following figure shows our plotted dataset before and after applying SMOTE oversampling algorithm.

![](assets/figure-09-e0c8efe9ef4225ea98e0266c.png)

Figure : Before (left graph) and after (right graph) applying SMOTE oversampling technique

In the above figure, the left side graph shows our plotted data points before applying SMOTE oversampling algorithm. The yellow color plotted points are majority classes and green and violet color plotted data points are minority classes. After applying SMOTE over sampling algorithm, in the right graph, we see that minority classes (green and violet color plotted data) have been increased in number by adding synthetic data points.

For overall experiment, we have used pipeline method from imbalanced learn api. The reason we have used pipeline method is that pipeline method performs three major tasks (oversampling, classification, and providing classification summary) sequentially.

We have applied both SMOTE and Borderline SMOTE algorithms on our minority observations. The following diagram shows the differences between these two oversampling algorithms in synthetic data points creation level.

![](assets/figure-10-e6cb678c29c1f571b05dca1e.png)

Figure : Oversampling using SMOTE (left) and Borderline SMOTE (right)

In the above diagram, we have applied oversampling technique (SMOTE and Borderline SMOTE) on a dataset that contains 2500 observations. It is clear from these two diagrams is that SMOTE generates more data points than Borderline SMOTE. According to the borderline SMOTE definition, it generates synthetic data points that are closer to each other compared to SMOTE algorithm.

After applying oversampling technique on our minority class from our initial dataset that contains 2500 observations, we have applied Linear SVM classification model to classify our data. The following figure shows the decision boundary as well as decision function for SMOTE.

![](assets/figure-11-dbf1954323893316e9f9524b.png)

Figure: Decision function after classifying SMOTE oversampled data

The above diagram explains classification boundary or decision boundary or decision function for both SMOTE and Borderline SMOTE oversampled data. According to the decision function, after classifying these two oversampled data, in the first diagram, we see that the decision boundary for majority plotted data points cannot separate the majority data points properly compared to the second diagram. In results and discussion section, we will show the confusion matrix, precision, and recall for the above classification. We will also show the classification result for different dataset.

Up to this point, we have oversampled and classified our first dataset that contains 2500 observations. Now we are going to work with a different dataset that contains 90,000 observations. The similar procedures that we applied on our first dataset that contains 2500 observations, are also applied on our new dataset.

![](assets/figure-12-d0a6ced50fbc968995244aa9.png)

Figure: 

**9.** **RESULTS AND DISCUSSIONS:**

In this section, we are going to evaluate the Linear SVM classification results. After applying two oversampling technique and Linear SVM algorithm for two different size datasets, we have classification details (accuracy, precision, and recall) for both datasets. First of all, we will look for the classification results for our first dataset that contains 2500 observations. The following table shows precision and recall value after oversampling using SMOTE and applying Linear SVM classification.

Table 1: 

|  | Precision | Recall |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 0.11 | 0.45 |
| 1 | 0.84 | 0.68 |
| 2 | 0.93 | 0.54 |
From the above table, we see that for class label 2, the precision rate is really high and the recall rate is low comparatively. We know that precision illustrates the correctness value in case of positive prediction. On the other hand, recall illustrates the total number of observations in our oversampled dataset that have been predicted correctly after applying a classification algorithm. Table 1 shows that the precision rate for class label 2 is 93 percent. The following normalize confusion matrix also shows the relationship between predicted label and true label.

![](assets/figure-13-f0eb131ae6e0928c5dd52cf5.png)

Figure : Confusion matrix for class label 2.

The overall accuracy of our training model up to this point is 96 percent. After providing few new data for prediction, the prediction shows up as 71 percent which clearly points out that there is an overfitting issue with the classification on our first dataset that contains 2500 observations.

In order to verify that whether the overfitting issue generated due to the dataset that contains small number of observations, we choose another imbalanced toy dataset that contains 90,000 observations. We followed the similar procedure for classification. First of all, we oversampled the minority observations in our new dataset. The only difference is we choose a different oversampling algorithm called Borderline SMOTE this time and then classify our oversampled dataset using Linear SVM classifier. Table show our obtained classification details (precision and recall) for the new dataset.

Table 2:

|  | Precision | Recall |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 0.11 | 0.58 |
| 1 | 0.84 | 0.71 |
| 2 | 0.82 | 0.91 |
Table 2 shows the precision and recall value of oversampled data using Borderline SMOTE. Notice that, for class label 2, the previous precision and recall value was 93 percent and 54 percent where these values have changed to 82 percent and 91 percent after applying Borderline oversampling algorithm instead of SMOTE. Clearly, there is no overfitting problem exists in this case.

While we apply both SMOTE and Borderline SMOTE algorithms on a large imbalanced dataset, no overfitting issue arises after applying Linear SVM classification. After oversampling our second dataset and then classifying we obtained the following precision and recall value. Both of the oversampling algorithms work well in such case.

Table 2:

| 

|  | Precision | Recall |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 0.04 | 0.75 |
| 1 | 0.90 | 0.79 |
| 2 | 0.87 | 0.83 |
 | 

|  | Precision | Recall |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 0.11 | 0.68 |
| 1 | 0.84 | 0.71 |
| 2 | 0.92 | 0.83 |
 |
| --- | --- |
Table 11 shows the classification info after oversampling our large dataset using SMOTE algorithm and Table 12 shows the classification info after oversampling the dataset using Borderline SMOTE. While we apply SMOTE oversampling algorithm on a large imbalanced dataset, no overfitting issue arises after applying Linear SVM classification.

10. FUTURE STUDIES:

The oversampling algorithm SMOTE works well while our imbalanced dataset contains large number of observations and low dimensional data. When a dataset contains few features, then the dataset is known as low dimensional data. In most of the cases, while we classify an SMOTE oversampled imbalanced dataset, it does not reduce bias toward the classification in the majority class when data are high dimensional. Though is some cases, this issue can be resolved by parameter tuning while classifying the oversampled data. A future study can be conducted on oversampling and classifying a high dimensional dataset without facing the overfitting issue.

CONCLUSION:

To sum up, in our experiment section, we have shown the details approach of identifying the overfitting issue for a comparatively small imbalanced dataset while we first oversample the minority class from our dataset and then classify the oversampled data. Finding such overfitting problem using multiple dataset can be defined as state of the art approach. Later, in our results and discussions section, we have identified the particular situation when the overfitting issue arises. Although there is not any specific and widely used approach to solve such overfitting issue for imbalanced dataset, we have shown that applying a different type of oversampling algorithm called Borderline SMOTE, we can overcome the overfitting problem for a small dataset. At the beginning of this report, we have mentioned the necessary tools and language that have been used in the project. The details instruction to compile and run the project source code have been added in appendix section including the major code block with proper comment.

notes.content:
## A security workflow with two levels of orchestration

This example automates an employee offboarding and security-risk audit. An orchestrator creates two bounded work items, each worker performs a small audit, and Python joins the results before a final model call writes the manifest.

The implementation is in [`orchestrator_parallel_pipeline.py`](../../../../orchestrator_parallel_pipeline.py), with deterministic unit tests in [`test_orchestrator_parallel_pipeline.py`](../../../../test_orchestrator_parallel_pipeline.py).

## The architecture

```text
                       [USER REQUEST]
"Offboard User: Alex Rivera (Engineering) & Audit Exposure"
                             ↓
             ┌───────────────────────────────┐
             │    STAGE 1: ORCHESTRATOR      │
             │   - Parses core request       │
             │   - Generates task matrix     │
             └───────────────────────────────┘
                             ↓
       ┌─────────────────────┴─────────────────────┐
       ▼ (Task 1)                                  ▼ (Task 2)
 ┌──────────────┐                            ┌──────────────┐
 │ WORKER 1: IT │                            │  WORKER 2:   │
 │ ACCESS AUDIT │                            │ SECURITY RISK│
 └──────┬───────┘                            └──────┬───────┘
        │                                           │
        ▼                                           ▼
 [FAN-OUT PARALLEL CHECK]                    [FAN-OUT PARALLEL CHECK]
 ├── Check GitHub Access                     ├── Audit Secret Leaks
 ├── Check AWS IAM Roles                     ├── Audit Data Exports
 └── Check Slack Provisioning                └── Audit Shadow IT
        │                                           │
        └────────────────────┬──────────────────────┘
                             ▼
             ┌───────────────────────────────┐
             │      STAGE 3: QUALITY GATE    │
             │ - Python: Joins parallel work │
             │ - Strips non-actionable rows  │
             └───────────────────────────────┘
                             ↓
             ┌───────────────────────────────┐
             │    STAGE 4: SYNTHESIZER       │
             │ - Compiles executive brief    │
             │ - Generates secure JSON manifest│
             └───────────────────────────────┘
                             ↓
                 [COMPLETED OFFBOARDING MANIFEST]
```

The key boundary is deliberate: the model suggests findings, while Python controls task structure, concurrency, provenance, and the quality filter. This is useful for security work because an empty or conversational model line does not become an action item accidentally.

## Stage 1: decompose the request

The profile is ordinary data, not executable instructions. `build_worker_tasks()` converts it into exactly two prompts:

```python
def build_worker_tasks(employee_profile: dict) -> dict:
    """Create the two bounded audit prompts for the employee profile."""
    role = employee_profile["role"]
    department = employee_profile["department"]
    return {
        "IT_Access_Worker": (
            f"Identify system access for {role} in {department}. "
            "Focus on GitHub, AWS, and production servers."
        ),
        "Security_Risk_Worker": (
            f"Identify exfiltration vectors for {role}. "
            "Focus on database dumps, configuration secrets, and API keys."
        ),
    }
```

The real module includes the full prompt wording and keeps the worker names stable so the fan-in report can retain source provenance.

## Stage 2: nested parallel fan-out

Each worker is an independent model call. `ThreadPoolExecutor` lets the two calls overlap, while the worker prompts remain small enough for a local 1.3B model to follow:

```python
with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=2) as executor:
    futures = {
        executor.submit(model_runner, prompt): worker_name
        for worker_name, prompt in worker_tasks.items()
    }
    for future, worker_name in futures.items():
        parallel_results[worker_name] = future.result()
        print(f"  ↳ Worker [{worker_name}] execution complete.")
```

`model_runner` is injectable. A production run uses `mlx-community/SmolLM2-1.3B-Instruct-4bit`; tests pass a deterministic function instead. The model import is lazy, so importing the module does not require Metal hardware.

## Stage 3: fan-in quality gate

The join is plain Python. It keeps the worker label, splits output into lines, and removes short conversational fragments:

```python
def quality_gate(parallel_results: dict) -> list[dict]:
    """Keep actionable worker lines and preserve their worker provenance."""
    aggregated = []
    for worker_name, output in parallel_results.items():
        clean_lines = [
            line.strip()
            for line in output.splitlines()
            if len(line.strip()) > MIN_FINDING_LENGTH
        ]
        aggregated.append({
            "source_worker": worker_name,
            "verified_findings": clean_lines,
        })
    return aggregated
```

This is not a claim that a finding is factually true. “Verified” here means it passed the programmatic shape and usefulness gate. Real access revocation still needs an approved integration and human review.

## Stage 4: synthesize the manifest

The synthesizer receives the strategic plan and JSON-encoded, filtered worker results. It is asked for two explicit sections: `ACTION ITEMS` and `RISK MITIGATION`.

```python
validated_payload = json.dumps(quality_gate(parallel_results), indent=2)
final_manifest = model_runner(
    "Create an Offboarding & Risk Management Manifest in Markdown with "
    f"ACTION ITEMS and RISK MITIGATION.\n{validated_payload}"
)
```

The returned object also includes the employee profile, strategic plan, and structured worker results. That makes the result inspectable before a downstream system decides whether to act.

## Unit testing without local-model hardware

The tests cover the architecture rather than the model’s prose quality:

```python
def fake_runner(prompt: str) -> str:
    """Return stable output for each model stage."""
    if "exactly two subtasks" in prompt:
        return "1. Access de-provisioning\n2. Security exposure audit"
    if "database dumps" in prompt:
        return "- Review database dump permissions\n- Rotate API access keys"
    if "GitHub" in prompt:
        return "- Revoke GitHub access\n- Remove AWS administrator role"

    return "# Offboarding Manifest\n\n## ACTION ITEMS\nRevoke access and rotate secrets."
```

The assertions check both branches, the filtering rule, the four model-stage calls, and that worker calls run on pool threads. This makes the concurrency and fan-in behavior testable even when MLX cannot load a device.

## Running and debugging

Run the deterministic unit tests from the repository root:

```bash
python -m unittest -v test_orchestrator_parallel_pipeline.py
```

For a real local-model run on a supported Apple Silicon environment:

```bash
python orchestrator_parallel_pipeline.py
```

The model path is lazy and isolated in `load_local_model()`. If the real run fails before the stage logs, check MLX and Metal availability. If it fails after worker completion, inspect the worker output and the JSON payload passed through `quality_gate()`.

The following output is from the unit test command above; it is a deterministic test-double run, not a live SmolLM2 generation:

```text
test_pipeline_runs_workers_and_synthesizes_manifest (test_orchestrator_parallel_pipeline.OrchestratorPipelineTests.test_pipeline_runs_workers_and_synthesizes_manifest) ... ok
test_quality_gate_strips_short_non_actionable_rows (test_orchestrator_parallel_pipeline.OrchestratorPipelineTests.test_quality_gate_strips_short_non_actionable_rows) ... ok
test_worker_tasks_cover_both_audit_branches (test_orchestrator_parallel_pipeline.OrchestratorPipelineTests.test_worker_tasks_cover_both_audit_branches) ... ok

----------------------------------------------------------------------
Ran 3 tests in 0.001s

OK
[1/4] Orchestrator: analyzing profile and breaking down audit tasks...
[2/4] Orchestrator: spawning specialized workers in parallel...
  ↳ Worker [IT_Access_Worker] execution complete.
  ↳ Worker [Security_Risk_Worker] execution complete.
[3/4] Running operational quality gate (Python fan-in)...
[4/4] Orchestrator synthesizer: building final offboarding manifest...
```
