notes.title: How a Traditional backend-for-frontend (BFF) Becomes a Practical Starting Point for AI Agents - AI BFF
notes.content:
# How a Traditional backend-for-frontend (BFF) Becomes a Practical Starting Point for AI Agents - AI BFF

---

A BFF adapts backend services to the needs of a particular interface. It gathers data, manages sessions, and exposes operations that match the product experience.

An AI agent needs a similar adaptation layer: focused tools, limited permissions, compact results, and predictable execution. This makes an existing BFF a practical starting point for agent features.

The extension is sometimes described as a **Backend for Agents (BFA)** or **Agent BFF**. These are architectural labels rather than a requirement to adopt a new framework. The useful idea is to carry established backend controls into a system where a model proposes actions.

# Start with the traditional BFF

Consider a customer-support application. Its order screen needs customer details from CRM, delivery status from an order service, and payment information from billing.

A BFF can combine those calls into one operation, such as `GET /api/orders/4821/summary`. The browser receives a response designed for that screen, while service-specific details remain behind the BFF.

This layer also gives the application a place to manage authentication, translate backend errors, and apply request limits. The core services remain responsible for their own business rules and resource-level authorization.

# Authentication establishes the foundation

In a server-managed BFF design, login uses OpenID Connect for identity and OAuth for API access. The BFF completes the authorization flow and retains access and refresh tokens on the server. The browser receives an opaque session cookie.

A typical cookie looks like this:

```http
Set-Cookie: __Host-session=<random-session-id>; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax
```

- **Secure** restricts transmission to HTTPS.

- **HttpOnly** prevents browser JavaScript from reading the cookie.

- **SameSite** limits when cookies accompany cross-site requests; the policy must fit the login flow.

- **An opaque session ID** refers to server-side state rather than exposing API tokens.

The BFF uses the session to identify the caller and selects the appropriate credentials for downstream calls. Session expiry, rotation, and logout remain part of the implementation.

This is one established browser architecture; browser applications can also use other OAuth designs. Its particular advantage is keeping API tokens out of browser JavaScript. [OAuth browser application guidance](https://www.ietf.org/ietf-ftp/rfc/rfc10017.html)

# XSS and CSRF need separate controls

**Cross-site scripting (XSS)** occurs when attacker-controlled content executes as script inside an application. Keeping tokens server-side reduces token theft, but malicious script can still make requests through an active session or read displayed data. Safe rendering, output encoding, dependency hygiene, and a restrictive Content Security Policy still matter.

**Cross-site request forgery (CSRF)** attempts to make an authenticated browser send an unwanted request. Because cookies can be attached automatically, a cookie-based BFF needs CSRF protection on state-changing operations: a validated CSRF token or another robust request-validation design, supported by Origin checks and an appropriate SameSite policy.

For example, `POST /api/refunds` must validate the session, request origin protections, and permission to refund the specific order. Merely hiding the refund button provides no backend protection.

These concerns carry directly into agent interfaces. Generated Markdown must be rendered safely, and an approval button must call a protected endpoint.

# Nginx handles the edge

Nginx can terminate HTTPS, route `/api/` requests to the BFF, enforce request-size limits, and apply coarse rate limits. The BFF then handles application-specific permissions and response shaping.

For example, Nginx can limit incoming requests, but the application decides whether a support employee may access a particular customer record. An API gateway can perform similar edge functions; neither replaces business authorization.

A same-origin deployment—browser application and BFF served under one site—also simplifies cookie handling and cross-origin configuration. The trusted proxy chain must be configured correctly so client-supplied forwarding headers cannot establish identity.

# Extend the design with two agent responsibilities

An agent feature introduces two distinct needs:

| Layer | Responsibility | Example |
| - | - | - |
| UI BFF | Connect people to agent runs | Start a run, stream progress, accept approval |
| Agent runtime | Coordinate model calls and workflow state | Choose a tool, inspect its result, continue |
| Agent tool boundary | Adapt backend operations for agent use | Validate a refund request and call billing |

The UI BFF and tool boundary can begin as separate modules in one service. Independent deployments become useful when scaling, ownership, or isolation requirements differ.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    UI["Browser or mobile UI"] -->|"HTTPS and session"| EDGE["Nginx or gateway"]
    EDGE --> BFF["UI BFF"]
    BFF -->|"Start and inspect runs"| RUN["Agent runtime and workers"]
    RUN -->|"Validated tool requests"| TOOL["Agent tool boundary"]
    TOOL --> CRM["CRM"]
    TOOL --> BILL["Billing"]
    BFF --> STATE["Run state and event store"]
    RUN --> STATE
    TOOL --> STATE
```

The diagram shows responsibility boundaries. Authentication and authorization also apply to internal calls, including access to run state.

# Turn backend capabilities into focused tools

A support agent asked to “check whether order 4821 can be refunded” should receive an operation aligned with that task:

```text
get_refund_eligibility(order_id)
```

The implementation checks access to the order, gathers payment and delivery information, and asks the relevant business service to evaluate eligibility. A compact result might be:

```json
{
  "order_id": "4821",
  "eligible": true,
  "maximum_refund": {"amount": "49.00", "currency": "CAD"},
  "reason": "Within the return window",
  "approval_required": true
}
```

This result preserves the facts needed for the next decision without returning unrelated customer data or internal service payloads.

A separate `issue_refund` tool performs the write. It validates arguments, checks authorization and approval, and rechecks eligibility before execution. The model proposes the action; trusted application code decides whether it can proceed.

Purpose-built tools are a useful default for business operations. General SQL or HTTP tools require additional isolation, restricted destinations or datasets, and execution limits.

# MCP exposes tools but does not supply business policy

**Model Context Protocol (MCP)** provides a standard interface through which compatible agent clients can discover and invoke tools. An MCP server can implement the agent tool boundary, while ordinary functions or REST endpoints can serve the same architectural role.

MCP does not automatically enforce tenant boundaries, refund limits, approvals, or safe retries. Those controls belong in the implementation and downstream services.

For authenticated remote HTTP deployments, validate token audience and permissions. A token issued for the MCP server must not simply be forwarded to another API as though it were issued for that API. MCP explicitly prohibits token passthrough. [MCP security guidance](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/2025-11-25/tutorials/security/security_best_practices)

# Keep credentials and authority outside model context

API keys, access tokens, and refresh tokens belong in protected server-side storage and credential-handling code. Exclude them from prompts, tool results, logs, and any files or environment variables accessible to model-controlled execution.

That reduces credential exposure, but prompt injection can still induce misuse of an allowed tool. Narrow permissions, resource checks, output controls, and approvals remain necessary.

When an agent acts for a person, preserve both the human identity and the agent or service identity. Where the identity provider supports it, the backend can request a short-lived token for a specific downstream API with limited scopes.

The authorization server issues that token; the BFF requests it. OAuth token exchange is a separate mechanism defined by RFC 8693, rather than a capability automatically provided by OAuth 2.1. A scope such as `orders:read` must still be combined with checks on which orders the caller may access. [OAuth token exchange](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8693)

# Make agent work independent of the browser connection

A multi-step task may outlast an ordinary HTTP request. A useful design separates starting work from observing it:

| Endpoint | Purpose |
| - | - |
| `POST /api/agent/runs` | Validate the request, persist and enqueue work, return `202 Accepted` with a run ID |
| `GET /api/agent/runs/{id}` | Read current status and available results |
| `GET /api/agent/runs/{id}/events` | Stream progress through Server-Sent Events |
| `POST /api/agent/runs/{id}/approvals` | Submit a decision for one pending action |
| `POST /api/agent/runs/{id}/cancel` | Request cancellation |

Every endpoint checks access to the run. A run ID is a reference, not proof of permission.

Server-Sent Events (SSE) carries updates from server to browser while ordinary POST requests handle decisions. WebSockets are an alternative when continuous two-way messaging is needed.

Stream useful events such as “Checking payment status,” `approval_required`, and `completed`. Internal model reasoning does not need to be exposed.

For reconnection, persist events with ordered IDs and replay retained events after `Last-Event-ID`. A fresh page load may need a persisted cursor or status refresh. Define a recovery response when older events have expired. SSE provides the transport; workers and durable storage provide continued execution. [SSE behavior](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Server-sent_events/Using_server-sent_events)

# Make approval an enforceable operation

An approval screen should show the exact action: the order, refund amount, currency, and consequence.

The runtime persists a pending action and pauses. The UI BFF accepts an authenticated, CSRF-protected decision. The backend verifies the approver’s permissions and binds approval to that action’s immutable arguments, run, and expiry.

Changing the amount requires fresh approval. Repeated clicks must not repeat the refund. Use an idempotency key and downstream deduplication, and recheck business conditions immediately before execution.

Redis can support sessions and event delivery, while a database or durable workflow store can retain runs and approvals. Storage choices depend on retention and recovery requirements; paused work must survive the failures the service promises to tolerate.

# Adapt Nginx for streaming

The following location fragment belongs inside an existing HTTPS server configuration. It assumes the BFF exposes the SSE route shown earlier and that Nginx is the direct TLS edge.

```nginx
location ~ ^/api/agent/runs/[^/]+/events$ {
    proxy_pass http://bff-service:3000;
    proxy_http_version 1.1;

    # Deliver events as the upstream produces them.
    proxy_buffering off;
    proxy_cache off;

    # Maximum idle interval between upstream reads.
    proxy_read_timeout 300s;

    proxy_set_header Host $host;
    proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
    proxy_set_header Connection "";
}
```

The application must send `Content-Type: text/event-stream`, flush events promptly, and use an appropriate cache policy. Periodic heartbeat comments keep quiet streams active.

The read timeout measures inactivity between reads, not total run duration. Load balancers and CDNs need compatible settings too. The forwarding headers shown are request metadata, not XSS or CSRF protection. [Nginx proxy documentation](https://nginx.org/en/docs/http/ngx_http_proxy_module.html)

# Retain the operational controls that make the boundary useful

- **Bound execution:** limit run duration, tool calls, model tokens, concurrent jobs, and downstream requests.

- **Minimize data:** return necessary fields, protect sensitive information, and apply access filters before retrieval. Redaction is a supporting control, not a guarantee.

- **Separate state:** chat history, retrieved context, workflow state, and credentials have different retention and access requirements.

- **Handle uncertain writes:** retry transient failures carefully; reconcile an ambiguous payment response before attempting another write.

- **Trace decisions:** record run ID, actor, tool, policy outcome, approval, and downstream result without logging secrets.

A useful first increment is a read-only agent behind the existing BFF, with a small tool set and observable runs. Write actions can follow once authorization, approval, and retry behavior are established.

The traditional BFF already provides a place to adapt clients to backend services. Extending it for agents means making proposed actions explicit, permissions enforceable, and long-running work recoverable.

notes.title: Building a Local-First Cognitive Memory Architecture for OpenAI Codex CLI
notes.summary: A local cognitive memory architecture combining working context, rules, workflows, semantic facts and episodic history.
notes.content: # Building a Local-First Cognitive Memory Architecture for OpenAI Codex CLI Modern AI coding agents like **OpenAI Codex CLI** are remarkably capable within a single context window, yet they suffer from session amnesia. Every new terminal session starts with a blank slate: architectural decisions made yesterday are forgotten, previously solved bug dead-ends are repeated, and standing repository conventions have to be re-explained. Assembling a **complete, local-first, five-tier cognitive memory system** solves this problem using Codex’s native configuration files and an open-source **Model Context Protocol (MCP)** memory server. Everything stays on the local machine—backed by plain Markdown and SQLite—with local embeddings and zero external network calls. --- ## 1. The Five Cognitive Memory Types in Software Engineering To keep an agent fast and prevent context-window bloat, notes should not be dumped into a single flat database. Borrowing from cognitive science, effective agent memory separates information by **lifespan, mutability, and retrieval pattern**: | Memory Type | Software Dev Equivalent | Lifespan | How It Enters Context | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **1. Short-Term (Working)** | Active diffs, current stack traces, immediate sub-tasks | Single session | Always present in active tokens; discarded on exit | | **2. Strategic (Rules)** | Coding style, test commands, security guardrails | Permanent (until edited) | Auto-injected on every turn via `AGENTS.md` | | **3. Procedural (Workflows)** | Release checklists, migration playbooks, debugging steps | Permanent (until edited) | Loaded on demand via `SKILL.md` triggers | | **4. Semantic (Facts)** | System architecture, API contracts, domain models | Long-term | Retrieved via local vector/FTS search when relevant | | **5. Episodic (History)** | Dated bug post-mortems, failed experiments, session logs | Append-only history | Retrieved by project tag, timestamp, or error similarity | --- ## 2. System Architecture: How the Pieces Connect Codex CLI acts as the central reasoning engine and communicates directly with local storage over **stdio** using MCP. ### Why This Stack Works * **Declarative Configuration:** Codex natively discovers `AGENTS.md` and `SKILL.md` files and spawns the MCP server automatically via `uvx`. * **Human-Readable & Git-Friendly:** Using **Basic Memory** (`basic-memory`), semantic and episodic memories are stored as standard Markdown files on disk, making them easy to inspect, edit, or `git commit` alongside source code. * **Sub-Millisecond Hybrid Search:** Behind the Markdown files, the MCP server maintains a local SQLite database combining **FTS5 (Full-Text Search)** for exact function and error matches with **local vector embeddings** for conceptual queries. --- ## 3. How Local Embeddings Work Under the Hood When Codex queries long-term memory, it often searches by concept rather than exact keyword (for example, *"how token refresh failures are handled"*). This pipeline executes completely offline: 1. **File Watching & Chunking:** Whenever a Markdown note is created or edited (either by Codex via MCP or directly in a text editor), the local MCP server splits the document into semantic chunks based on Markdown headings. 2. **Local Model Inference:** The server passes each chunk through a lightweight local embedding model—typically an ONNX-quantized model like `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` or `bge-small-en-v1.5` (roughly 80–130 MB), or a local **Ollama** model (`nomic-embed-text`). On first launch, the model downloads once to `~/.cache/` and runs on CPU or Apple Silicon GPU in milliseconds. 3. **Vector + FTS5 Indexing:** The resulting numerical vector and raw text tokens are written into a local SQLite database. 4. **Hybrid Retrieval:** When Codex calls `search_notes`, the query is embedded locally, compared against stored vectors via cosine similarity, blended with BM25 keyword scores, and only the top 3–5 relevant snippets are returned into Codex's context window. *(Note: For setups that skip neural models altogether, tools like `codex-agent-mem` rely purely on SQLite FTS5 keyword ranking, which is near-instant and well-suited for searching exact symbol names and error codes.)* --- ## 4. Step-by-Step Implementation Guide ### Step 1: Prerequisites Ensure **Codex CLI** is installed and **`uv`** (Astral's fast Python package runner) is available on the system so Codex can launch Python MCP servers in isolated environments without polluting global dependencies. ```bash # Install uv (macOS / Linux) curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh ``` ### Step 2: Create the Local Memory Vault Structure Create a dedicated directory on disk (or inside a shared development folder) to house long-term memory files cleanly separated by type: ```bash mkdir -p ~/dev-memory/semantic mkdir -p ~/dev-memory/episodic ``` * `~/dev-memory/semantic/` holds timeless architecture docs, database schemas, and integration contracts. * `~/dev-memory/episodic/` holds dated bug investigations, migration logs, and session summaries. ### Step 3: Register the MCP Server in Codex (`~/.codex/config.toml`) Open or create `~/.codex/config.toml` and register **Basic Memory** as a local MCP server pointing to the memory directory: ```toml # Enable Codex's lightweight native session recall alongside MCP [features] memories = true # Register local Python MCP server for Semantic & Episodic memory [mcp_servers.memory] command = "uvx" args = ["basic-memory", "mcp", "--project", "dev-memory"] env = { BASIC_MEMORY_HOME = "/Users/USERNAME/dev-memory" } ``` *(Replace `/Users/USERNAME/dev-memory` with the actual home directory path.)* ### Step 4: Configure Strategic Memory (`~/.codex/AGENTS.md`) Global `AGENTS.md` instructions are injected into every Codex session. This file defines universal engineering standards and instructs Codex **when and how** to read and write to the MCP memory server: ```markdown # Global Engineering Standards (Strategic Memory) ## Core Development Rules - Write clean, modular, well-typed code. - Always run the project test suite before concluding a task. - Never hardcode secrets, API keys, or environment-specific paths. ## Cognitive Memory Protocol A local `memory` MCP server backed by Markdown files in `semantic/` and `episodic/` is available. Follow this lifecycle strictly: 1. **Before Modifying Unfamiliar Code (Recall):** - Query `memory` for architectural decisions (`semantic/`) and past bug post-mortems (`episodic/`) related to the target module or repository name. 2. **During Active Implementation (Short-Term):** - Keep working hypotheses, raw stack traces, and temporary diffs in the active session only. Do not pollute long-term memory with unverified guesses. 3. **After Solving Non-Trivial Problems (Consolidation):** - **Architectural / Design Decisions:** Save or update a timeless note under `semantic/-.md` documenting the final design, trade-offs, and invariants. - **Bug Fixes & Dead Ends:** Save a dated log under `episodic/YYYY-MM-DD--.md` recording the symptom, root cause, rejected approaches, and verified fix. ``` ### Step 5: Add Procedural Memory via Skills (`.codex/skills/`) For multi-step workflows needed only occasionally (such as database migrations or release checks), create a **Codex Skill** inside the repository so it does not consume tokens on unrelated turns: ```bash mkdir -p .codex/skills/db-migration ``` Create `.codex/skills/db-migration/SKILL.md`: ```markdown --- name: db-migration description: Safe workflow for creating, testing, and verifying database schema migrations. Trigger whenever modifying database models or SQL schemas. --- # Database Migration Procedure (Procedural Memory) 1. Query the `memory` MCP server under `episodic/` for any past migration lockups or rollback incidents in this repo. 2. Generate the migration script using the project's ORM CLI. 3. Inspect the generated SQL for destructive operations (`DROP COLUMN`, table locks). 4. Apply the migration to the local test database, run integration tests, and verify rollback (`downgrade`) works cleanly. 5. Record any non-obvious schema constraints in `semantic/-schema.md` via the `memory` MCP server. ``` --- ## 5. End-to-End Walkthrough: A Real Session in Action To illustrate how all five layers cooperate, consider a typical session debugging a recurring authentication issue: 1. **Session Initialization:** Running `codex` inside `~/projects/billing-api` automatically loads `~/.codex/AGENTS.md` (Strategic Memory) and indexes the YAML headers of `.codex/skills/*/SKILL.md` (Procedural Memory). 2. **Targeted Recall:** Given the prompt *"Users are getting random 401 errors during token refresh under load,"* Codex follows `AGENTS.md` and calls the `memory` MCP tool `search_notes("billing-api token refresh 401")`. 3. **Hybrid Retrieval:** The MCP server embeds the query locally, searches SQLite, and returns two snippets: * `semantic/billing-api-auth.md` (explaining how Redis stores refresh token rotation locks). * `episodic/2026-09-14-billing-api-redis-timeout.md` (noting a past connection-pool exhaustion bug). 4. **Short-Term Execution:** Armed with prior context, Codex inspects the auth middleware, reproduces the race condition in its active context window (Short-Term Memory), and applies a fix. 5. **Memory Consolidation:** Before finishing, Codex calls `write_note` to create `episodic/2026-11-15-billing-api-refresh-race.md` with the root cause and fix, and updates `semantic/billing-api-auth.md` with the new locking invariant. The MCP server immediately indexes both Markdown files for future sessions. --- ## 6. Best Practices & Maintenance Tips * **Keep Strategic Memory Lean:** Every line in `AGENTS.md` is paid for on every single turn. Keep it under 150 lines of crisp rules and push detailed reference docs into `semantic/` Markdown files. * **Tag Notes with Repository Names:** Always include the repository or service name in note titles and frontmatter so multi-project vaults do not cross-contaminate search results. * **Prune Stale Facts:** Because `semantic/` notes are plain Markdown files, spend five minutes once a month deleting obsolete architecture notes or merging duplicate episodic logs—or instruct Codex itself to audit and deduplicate `~/dev-memory/semantic/`. * **Protect Sensitive Data:** Never store `.env` values, tokens, or customer PII inside the memory vault, especially when syncing `~/dev-memory` via a private Git repository.

notes.title: Document ingestion pipeline overview
notes.content:
## Document ingestion pipeline overview ---
This small-scale pipeline helps me stream and organize different types of documents, for example, markdown files from local coding agents, reusable functions and refined web crawled data into a tidy, open-source knowledge base for AI agents.

It started to get hands-on practice building real-time RAG systems: - How to make the right decisions around solution approaches - How to choose the right libraries and databases - How to overcome common RAG pitfalls Data ingestion is divided into two primary modules: ### 1. Streaming AI generated markdown files --- - **Workflow documentation ingestion:** When local coding agents follow a structured workflow, for example: ``` Create plan │ ▼ Implement │ ▼ Validate │ ▼ Save plan & implementation summary (Markdown) ``` This can generate a large number of documents over time that can be useful for agents to learn from and allow them to reuse existing code (reusable functions) without rethinking and rewriting everything. A Python local-folder-watcher function automatically captures and streams those files. Additionally, files generated by web-chat agents can be streamed and used as well. When I say streaming, I mean it sends those files to a central S3 storage bucket. - **Reusable code and pattern indexing:** Periodically scans and ingests agent-generated code that has been reviewed, refined and dropped in a reusable function directory. ### 2. External web crawling --- - This module crawls external web pages using `crawl4ai` Python library and generate raw markdown files. - It strips away boilerplate HTML, navigation bars and ads during the crawl. The detailed approaches for both modules are explained in the next few docs.

notes.title: Streaming AI generated markdown files
notes.content:
## Streaming AI generated Markdown files ---
This central markdown file storage serves two main purposes: **1. Shared context across agents:** - These files are directly usable as agent context without having to worry about which agent created them. - For example, I can chat with ChatGPT about an architectural decision, and once I completely agree and decide on an approach, I can ask it to create a `plan.md` file and save it to S3 (a custom MCP plugin and skill will send the file to S3). - With an event-driven setup, a local Codex CLI agent can then get notified and start implementing the plan. Or simply invoke the coding agent manually for implementation. **2. Post-turn analysis and curated knowledge extraction:** - Analyzing and processing the files generated after each agent turn (e.g, plan and implementation summaries) and - Prepare a curated silver dataset containing repeatable development approaches, strategies, lessons learned and reusable functions/code files. These turn files can capture critical insights for future agents, such as: - Repeatable architectural decisions that can be applied to other problems - Debugging outcomes and key takeaways - Recurring bugs - Implementations that the user asked to apply differently - Tasks that required multiple back-and-forth chats and turns to complete ### Overall streaming workflow --- 1. Local coding agents (eg, Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode) write their generated Markdown files directly into the Local Knowledge Folder. 2. A Folder Watcher (running as a Python background thread) continuously monitors the folder for any file add, update, or delete events and sends those Markdown files to the MCP client. 3. Web and mobile agents (eg, ChatGPT and Claude) can also send documents directly through the same MCP client. 4. The MCP client sends requests secured with a Bearer token to AWS API Gateway for token validation. 5. Once validated, Lambda function (running Flask + FastMCP) validates the incoming payload and handles document storage. 6. Lambda stores the raw Markdown content in S3 bucket and writes the document metadata and index entries to DynamoDB.

notes.title: Web crawling and data processing overview
notes.content:
## Web crawling and data processing overview --- - A single-threaded `crawl4ai` instance crawls predefined web pages for knowledge and stores the raw data as markdown files. - After refinement, the file is dropped into a `refined` folder, which triggers the Python watcher to send the file to an AWS S3 bucket. - No advanced crawling mechanism is used—just a basic, on-demand crawler. ### Overall flow diagram ---

### Markdown review and cleaning --- - Review raw Markdown outputs from agent turns (plan and implementation summaries) and crawl4ai web scrapes before adding them to the shared knowledge base. - Strip out scraped web boilerplate, failed agent attempts, and conversational filler so only clean, high-signal context remains. - Refine turn summaries to highlight repeatable architectural decisions, debugging takeaways, recurring bugs, and preferred coding approaches. - Save the vetted files into the refined folder to trigger the Python watcher and sync ready-to-use Markdown context to AWS S3.

notes.title: How the runtime works
notes.content:
### Adaptive RAG memory and search pipeline overview --- This lightweight pipeline gives local coding agents (like Codex, Claude Code) a shared, persistent memory and a fast way to learn new documentation without stalling their coding loop.

It solve two common bottlenecks: - Avoiding repeated searches and token burn on problems the agent has already solved - Preventing slow, heavy web crawls from blocking the agent while it is actively writing code The system runs as an isolated FastMCP server inside a sandbox. It uses LangGraph and a Deep Agent architecture to orchestrate retrieval and background learning across three primary stages: #### 1. Memory-first planning and hybrid retrieval Before writing code or searching the web, the main CLI agent calls `request_memory_plan(task, codebase_context, skills)`. A Coordinator Agent manages the lookup flow: - Clarification before retrieval: If the task is ambiguous, the coordinator triggers an interrupt() to gather missing context first. - Multi-strategy lookup: memory-scout queries across dense vectors, BM25 keyword indexes and an AST code graph to catch both conceptual notes and exact function signatures. - Fast-fail on misses: If nothing relevant exists in memory, the server returns `status="memory_miss"` right away instead of forcing the agent to wait on a live scrape. #### 2. Dual-speed web search delegation When a memory miss occurs and the agent needs external docs or examples, it drafts its own initial plan and calls `delegate_web_search(queries, urls)`. Instead of choosing between speed and thoroughness, this tool splits the work into two parallel tracks: - Foreground (< 3–5s) — Fast Search Scout: Performs quick HTTP and snippet fetches to hand an immediate summary back to the CLI agent. Codex or Claude Code keeps coding with zero noticeable wait. - Background (Non-blocking) — Deep Archiver Subagent: Spawned asynchronously via `asyncio.create_task`, this worker runs a parallel Crawl4AI fleet to scrape full documentation pages without holding up the main thread. #### 3. Self-improving knowledge vault While the main agent finishes its current task, the Deep Archiver Subagent prepares the knowledge base for future runs: - Distills crawled web pages into clean Markdown files inside /vault/ - Parses code blocks into an AST representation and embeds them into ChromaDB The next time any agent faces a similar task, that freshly archived documentation is already indexed and ready to be served as a memory-backed blueprint.

notes.title: Evaluating the memory system using a 8-B coding model
notes.content:
### Evaluating the memory system using a 8-B coding model --- ##### Does RAG memory help Qwen3 8B write code? **Yes, when the task depends on an earlier project decision.** In 27 local completions across nine tasks, Qwen3 passed **31 of 33 behavioral checks with retrieved memory**, up from **19 of 33 without it**. Three more tasks passed every primary check. Eleven of the twelve added passes came from simulated project policies with values the baseline prompt left out. The three repository-derived tasks added one pass in total. #### How to read the evaluation --- - **Start with the retry schedule.** Open the context and model responses in the case explorer. The baseline generates generic exponential backoff. The memory-backed function uses the specific millisecond schedule and both bounds. - **Then try the handoff path.** The retriever finds the correct rule, yet the model rejects valid nested paths. This is a failure to implement the retrieved rule. - **Compare tasks or timing.** Use the task-group selector to distinguish repository contracts, simulated decisions, and controls. Use the metric selector for checks passed, tasks fully passed, duration, or prompt tokens.

#### Results --- The run used Ollama 0.40.17 on an Apple M2 with 16 GiB of memory. The installed tag was `qwen3:8b`, reported by the local API as 8.2B and Q4_K_M, with digest prefix `500a1f067a9f`. This is Qwen3 8B running coding tasks. The previously installed `qwen2.5-coder:3b` was outside the comparison. | Metric | No memory | Retrieved memory | Reference excerpt | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | | Behavioral checks passed | 19/33 (57.6%) | **31/33 (93.9%)** | 28/33 (84.8%) | | Tasks fully passed | 4/9 | **7/9** | 7/9 | | Median Ollama request | 3.71 s | 5.93 s | 5.55 s | | Median reported prompt tokens | 133 | 233 | 211 | | Median reported output tokens | 56 | 73 | 73 | | Task | No memory | Retrieved | Reference | Observed behavior | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- | | Digest compatibility | 4/4 | 4/4 | 4/4 | The conventional UTF-8 SHA-256 prefix worked in all conditions. | | Text decoder | 2/4 | 3/4 | 0/4 | Retrieved code led Qwen to use strict incremental decoding, though it also rejected valid whitespace. The reference answer generated a regex that failed at import. | | Handoff path | 3/4 | 3/4 | 3/4 | All three rejected valid nested paths. The evidence-backed answers incorrectly put the forward slash in a denylist. | | Notebook batch size | 1/4 | 4/4 | 4/4 | The retrieved answer used default 24 and bounds 3–96. | | Carousel retry schedule | 0/4 | 4/4 | 4/4 | The retrieved answer applied the exact pauses and capped attempt indices. | | Compact status codes | 0/4 | 4/4 | 4/4 | The retrieved answer used the fixed-width mapping, casing rule, and unknown fallback. | | Stable deduplication | 4/4 | 4/4 | 4/4 | Search returned no excerpts. The task was fully specified. | | Closed-interval merge | 4/4 | 4/4 | 4/4 | Search returned no excerpts. The task was fully specified. | | Unpublished spool code | 1/1 | 1/1 | 1/1 | The related note contained no exact value. All responses explicitly reported the missing policy. | #### What the retriever contributed --- - **It found the target first in all six tasks with a known source.** The benchmark passed the entire coordinator response to Qwen. The notebook and carousel lookups each returned one plausible competing note after the target. Qwen applied the current policy in both cases. The notebook’s current and archived excerpts had closely spaced fusion scores of 0.01639 and 0.01613. Source wording and precedence were more informative than the raw gap. - **It preserved details a generic answer could not infer.** Without memory, the notebook answer guessed a default of 100, the carousel answer assumed a 100 ms base, and the status answer invented a mapping. All three with-memory answers applied the stored project values. Across those three tasks, the score moved from **1/12 to 12/12**. Across the repository-derived tasks it moved from **9/12 to 10/12**. - **It could surface a relevant note even when the answer was unavailable.** The unpublished spool lookup returned a note about retention that explicitly said the exact spool code was unpublished. A search result established topical relevance. The model still had to determine whether the excerpt contained the requested answer. - **The retriever had little to add to self-contained Python tasks.** Both controls were 8/8 in total in every condition. Those two memory-on prompts had empty evidence lists because the live lookup returned no matches. #### Where context still failed --- - **Decode.** The retrieved answer used the correct strict UTF-8 API and its incomplete-tail behavior. Its simplified control-byte range denied tab and newlines. The reference answer copied a double-escaped raw byte pattern and raised `PatternError` when Python compiled it. The target evidence was available in both conditions. The generated implementation was the limiting step. - **Path.** The retrieved excerpt explicitly allowed forward slashes as separators. Both evidence-backed implementations denied them before checking the path components. Three rejection checks passed easily, masking the fact that valid nested paths failed. The acceptance check exposed the mistake. - **Batch.** The hand-picked reference answer passed all four primary checks but returned 1 and 2 unchanged, even though the policy floors both to 3. The retrieved answer clamped them correctly. Five checks were added after reviewing the outputs and run against the saved responses. They are excluded from the primary score above. | Post-run edge checks | No memory | Retrieved | Reference | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | | Decode at real EOF and with NUL | 0/2 | 2/2 | 0/2 | | Accept a simple nested path | 0/1 | 0/1 | 0/1 | | Floor small positive and negative batch sizes | 0/2 | 2/2 | 1/2 | Open **Post-run edge checks** in the explorer to see the failures. The reference condition provides a cleaner evidence input. Its score can still fall because the model must turn that input into working code. This run does not establish that competing excerpts improve generation. #### Speed and token usage --- - **Lookup was short on this index.** Warm hybrid lookup took **22 ms median** and **32 ms maximum**. Median lookup plus the Ollama request was **5.95 s**. - **The model took longer in a typical memory-backed request.** The two arm medians were **3.71 s** and **5.93 s**. Comparing each task with its own baseline, the median extra model time was **1.12 s**. These are two different summaries of the same timings. - **Output throughput was similar.** Ollama reported about **16 tokens/s** in all three arms. The memory arm processed more prompt tokens and generated more output tokens at the median. - **The retry case shows the trade-off.** Retrieval added 24 ms. The prompt grew from 134 to 494 input tokens, the model request took 2.97 s versus 7.57 s, and the score improved from 0/4 to 4/4. The compact-status case improved from 0/4 to 4/4 while the model request was slightly shorter. | Median per-request measurement | No memory | Retrieved memory | Reference excerpt | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | | Prompt evaluation (s) | 0.46 | 1.00 | 0.92 | | Output evaluation (s) | 3.59 | 4.81 | 4.64 | | Output throughput (tokens/s) | 16.3 | 16.0 | 16.6 | Each breakdown row is the median of its own per-request measurements. The component medians can come from different tasks. Output throughput is reported output tokens divided by Ollama's output evaluation time for each request. **Per-task measurements.** The seconds columns show Ollama request wall time. The lookup column measures hybrid retrieval separately and applies to the retrieved-memory condition. Token pairs are reported input/output counts. | Task | Lookup (ms) | No memory (s) | Retrieved (s) | Reference (s) | No memory in/out | Retrieved in/out | Reference in/out | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | | Digest compatibility | 32 | 3.71 | 3.59 | 4.36 | 133/56 | 224/45 | 196/45 | | Text decoder | 26 | 5.11 | 8.29 | 8.14 | 139/81 | 460/96 | 287/109 | | Handoff path | 23 | 6.65 | 12.63 | 11.50 | 132/102 | 259/186 | 242/176 | | Notebook batch size | 21 | 3.51 | 4.73 | 4.54 | 130/54 | 305/53 | 211/60 | | Carousel retry schedule | 24 | 2.97 | 7.57 | 5.55 | 134/41 | 494/78 | 218/78 | | Compact status codes | 21 | 6.26 | 5.93 | 5.68 | 127/93 | 233/73 | 220/73 | | Stable deduplication | 22 | 3.67 | 3.84 | 3.93 | 132/47 | 132/47 | 132/47 | | Closed-interval merge | 21 | 12.63 | 13.75 | 19.05 | 151/137 | 151/137 | 151/137 | | Unpublished spool code | 21 | 1.54 | 1.71 | 0.50 | 136/4 | 206/4 | 136/4 | #### My working estimate for local use --- - **Use it for exact project rules.** Small compatibility helpers, established configuration rules, and exact mappings are good candidates when a few assertions can verify the result. - **Expect little quality lift when the prompt already specifies the behavior.** Both general Python controls passed without retrieved evidence. - **Check ordinary valid inputs as well as invalid and boundary inputs.** The path validator passed three rejection checks while incorrectly rejecting valid nested paths. #### Exact prompts - System prompt used in every request --- ```text You write small standalone Python 3 functions. Return Python source only, with any required standard-library imports. Do not import the project. Use supplied memory as reference data, prioritizing the active project over drafts or other consumers. If a required exact project policy cannot be inferred or is unpublished, answer exactly MISSING_POLICY. Implement ordinary fully specified Python tasks without memory. ``` ##### Worked example with and without memory - **Fixed inputs.** The system message above and the task string below are identical in every condition for this task. - **Lookup inputs.** The runner sends the following query and phrases to the memory coordinator. Qwen receives the returned paths and excerpts in its user message. - **Payload format.** These blocks show the user message JSON with indentation added for readability. The actual user message contained the same JSON values in a single serialized string. ```json { "query": "Carousel adapter retry budget approved pause schedule in milliseconds.", "keywords": [ "carousel adapter", "retry budget", "pause schedule" ] } ``` ##### User message without memory ```json { "task": "Implement carousel_pause_ms(attempt: int) -> int following the carousel adapter's approved retry budget. Attempt is a zero-based index. Support all integer inputs.", "memory": [] } ``` ##### User message with retrieved memory ```json { "task": "Implement carousel_pause_ms(attempt: int) -> int following the carousel adapter's approved retry budget. Attempt is a zero-based index. Support all integer inputs.", "memory": [ { "path": "decisions/retry-budget.md", "excerpt": "[Document: retry-budget.md | Section: Carousel adapter retry budget]\n# Carousel adapter retry budget\nUse a zero-based failed attempt index. Negative attempts are treated as zero.\nThe accepted retry pause schedule in milliseconds is 180, 540, 1620, 2100.\nUse 2100 for every attempt index above three. Return an integer." }, { "path": "drafts/retry-backoff.md", "excerpt": "[Document: retry-backoff.md | Section: Default HTTP retry backoff]\n# Default HTTP retry backoff\nThe shared web client starts at 100 milliseconds and doubles its backoff after each\nfailed attempt, capped at 3000 milliseconds. The carousel adapter has its own schedule." }, { "path": "implementation-summary.md", "excerpt": "[Document: implementation-summary.md | Section: Prior implementation snapshots > Changed files]\n## Changed files \n- `utils.py` — Fixture snapshot\n- `embedding/decode_source.py` — Fixture snapshot\n- `planning/changed-file-path.md` — Fixture snapshot\n- `decisions/batch-size.md` — Fixture snapshot\n- `decisions/retry-budget.md` — Fixture snapshot\n- `decisions/compact-status.md` — Fixture snapshot\n- `drafts/admin-status.md` — Fixture snapshot\n- `drafts/retry-backoff.md` — Fixture snapshot\n- `drafts/batch-size-archive.md` — Fixture snapshot\n- `notes/spool-budget.md` — Fixture snapshot\n- `notes/chunking.md` — Fixture snapshot\n- `notes/exports.md` — Fixture snapshot" } ] } ``` The three excerpts arrived in the order shown. The accepted carousel schedule ranked first, followed by the general HTTP retry policy and a handoff file list. The hand-picked reference condition used the accepted schedule excerpt alone, without its retrieval header. ##### What Qwen returned **Without memory · 0/4 checks** ```python def carousel_pause_ms(attempt: int) -> int: if attempt < 0: return 0 return 100 * (2 ** attempt) ``` **With retrieved memory · 4/4 checks** ```python import math def carousel_pause_ms(attempt: int) -> int: attempt = max(0, attempt) if attempt < 4: pauses = [180, 540, 1620, 2100] return pauses[attempt] else: return 2100 ``` - **What changed.** Qwen replaced the guessed 100 ms base with the stored `[180, 540, 1620, 2100]` schedule. It clamped negative attempts to the first entry and used 2100 ms beyond the final index. - **How it was checked.** The four checks exercised the initial pause, a negative index, both intermediate entries, and the cap. #### All nine task and lookup prompts --- The task text below went into the `task` field unchanged across all three conditions. Queries and phrases were authored before generation and sent to the retriever separately. - **Digest compatibility** - **Task** “Implement digest_key(value: str, length: int) -> str as a standalone compatibility wrapper that produces the existing RAG memory store's short hash keys.” - **Lookup query** “Reuse sha256_hex for stable shortened memory handoff digest keys.” - **Keyword phrases** `sha256_hex`, `digest`, `hash` - **Retrieved sources in prompt order** `utils.py` - **Text decoder** - **Task** “Implement preview_text(raw: bytes, truncated: bool = False) -> str | None, compatible with the RAG memory loader's decoder for text, binary controls, and capped samples.” - **Lookup query** “Reuse decode_source UTF-8 code, binary controls and truncated sample handling from the file loader.” - **Keyword phrases** `decode_source`, `binary controls`, `truncated` - **Retrieved sources in prompt order** `embedding/decode_source.py`, `implementation-summary.md` - **Handoff path** - **Task** “Implement valid_snapshot_path(value: str) -> bool. Match the ChangedFile handoff validator's path restrictions on normalized input. Assume no surrounding whitespace.” - **Lookup query** “ChangedFile handoff path validator and allowed snapshot path components.” - **Keyword phrases** `ChangedFile`, `snapshot paths`, `path validation` - **Retrieved sources in prompt order** `planning/changed-file-path.md` - **Notebook batch size** - **Task** “Implement notebook_batch_size(value: int | None) -> int using the active project's batch limit for notebook import. Input parsing happens upstream.” - **Lookup query** “Current batch size limit for notebook import in the accepted implementation.” - **Keyword phrases** `notebook importer`, `batch limit`, `records per batch` - **Retrieved sources in prompt order** `decisions/batch-size.md`, `drafts/batch-size-archive.md` - **Carousel retry schedule** - **Task** “Implement carousel_pause_ms(attempt: int) -> int following the carousel adapter's approved retry budget. Attempt is a zero-based index. Support all integer inputs.” - **Lookup query** “Carousel adapter retry budget approved pause schedule in milliseconds.” - **Keyword phrases** `carousel adapter`, `retry budget`, `pause schedule` - **Retrieved sources in prompt order** `decisions/retry-budget.md`, `drafts/retry-backoff.md`, `implementation-summary.md` - **Compact status codes** - **Task** “Implement compact_status(status: str) -> str using the existing compact export status codes, including normalization and fallback for new statuses.” - **Lookup query** “Compact export status fixed width reader mapping and unknown fallback.” - **Keyword phrases** `compact export`, `status codes`, `fixed-width` - **Retrieved sources in prompt order** `decisions/compact-status.md` - **Stable deduplication** - **Task** “Implement unique_in_order(items: list[str]) -> list[str]. Keep the first occurrence of each exact string in input order. Leave the input unchanged.” - **Lookup query** “Stable exact string deduplication in arrival order in Python.” - **Keyword phrases** `deduplicate`, `first occurrence`, `unique_in_order` - **Retrieved sources in prompt order** No excerpts - **Closed-interval merge** - **Task** “Implement merge_windows(windows: list[tuple[int, int]]) -> list[tuple[int, int]]. Assume valid closed intervals. Sort by start, merge overlaps including shared endpoints, and leave the input unchanged. Adjacent disjoint intervals stay separate.” - **Lookup query** “Merge sorted closed intervals sharing an endpoint in Python.” - **Keyword phrases** `merge_windows`, `closed intervals`, `shared endpoint` - **Retrieved sources in prompt order** No excerpts - **Unpublished spool code** - **Task** “Implement nightly_spool_code() -> str using the project's exact published nightly handoff spool code. The caller needs an exact value and cannot accept an invented default.” - **Lookup query** “Find the exact published nightly handoff spool code for archive spool records.” - **Keyword phrases** `nightly handoff`, `spool code`, `archive spool` - **Retrieved sources in prompt order** `notes/spool-budget.md` #### Methodology --- ##### What goes into each prompt Each task asks for one standalone Python helper. All three conditions receive the same instructions and task. The runner changes only the evidence list. It makes a fresh Ollama chat request each time, with no conversation history, repository tools, or previous generated answer. | Condition | Evidence | | --- | --- | | No memory | Empty list. The model uses the task text and its existing knowledge. | | Retrieved memory | All excerpts returned by the project’s memory coordinator, in the same order. | | Reference excerpt | One hand-picked source for each of the six evidence-bearing tasks. The three controls get an empty list. This is a clean-context diagnostic. | Each lookup gets a prewritten standalone query and a separate list of keyword phrases, just as it would from a calling coding agent. This measures retrieval given those queries. It does not test an 8B model’s ability to choose when to search or formulate its own queries. #### Where the context comes from --- The runner creates a temporary profile from the repository’s default configuration before importing project code. It pins the index paths inside that profile and uses local embeddings. It records the fixture as a task handoff through the production coordinator, using a frozen set of three repository-derived excerpts, three simulated accepted decisions, and six supporting or competing notes. A generated handoff summary is also indexed. The fixture includes only material intended for this benchmark. The index contained **13 indexed files**, **16 chunks**, and **7 graph edges**. Those counts include the generated handoff summary. 1. The handoff writes a summary and source snapshots into the temporary vault. 2. The embedding pipeline chunks the files, embeds them with local `all-MiniLM-L6-v2`, and indexes the chunks in Chroma and SQLite. 3. The memory coordinator searches code and docs separately. It uses Chroma vector similarity and SQLite FTS5 BM25 phrase queries. Reciprocal rank fusion weights their ranks 0.6 and 0.4 respectively, with a smoothing constant of 60. 4. The coordinator allows up to four ranked results per collection and up to two graph neighbors per collection. Code results precede docs in the combined response. Prompt positions in the report describe that concatenated list. A rank-fusion score is an ordering signal within the search, not a probability that the excerpt answers the task. 5. The runner passes each returned path and excerpt to Qwen. The temporary profile is deleted after retrieval. The trial uses the same coordinator as MCP’s memory lookup, invoked directly so server startup and transport are outside the measured lookup time. #### How answers are scored --- Eight coding tasks have four named checks each. One unpublished-policy control has a single check for an exact `MISSING_POLICY` response. For the coding tasks, the runner removes a single enclosing Python fence when present. It runs the answer with an allowlisted Python environment inside a separate macOS sandboxed process with CPU and wall-time limits. The tests call the returned functions on fixed inputs and compare outputs. This is an execution score, with no model judging another model. A task fully passes when every check passes. A partial score weights the checks equally and indicates where behavior broke. The nine tasks were authored for this benchmark. Six involve a known source, two specify general Python behavior directly, and one requires the model to acknowledge an unpublished policy. Several checks on the same helper are related, so 33 checks are still evidence from nine tasks. A separate post-run audit adds five input-boundary checks across three tasks after inspecting the generated responses. These results are shown separately and do not affect the 33-check primary score. The runner also records: - **Target coverage.** Whether the expected source path appeared anywhere in the returned prompt. This does not measure the judged relevance of every other excerpt. - **Lookup time.** Warm in-process coordinator wall time, after the fixture is indexed. Indexing and network transport are outside this interval. - **Generation time.** Wall time around the local Ollama request, including prompt processing and response generation. Grading and retrieval are outside this interval. A separate model warmup ran first. - **Token counts.** Ollama’s reported input and output counts. Prompt characters are preserved separately in the raw run. Generation uses `temperature=0`, seed 42, thinking off, an 8,192-token context window and up to 480 generated tokens. The runner shuffles the three conditions within each task using a fixed random seed. Prompt caching, machine activity, and output length can still affect timing. Timing values describe this host and run. #### Limitations and follow-up --- The trial measures whether a small model can write a few correct lines after receiving local precedent. Some baseline tasks intentionally omit project-specific values, making them a test of recall and use of evidence. Three source snapshots are repository-derived. The three novel policies and the archived alternatives are synthetic. The corpus is small and contains several distinctive strings, so coverage here is likely easier than in a noisy accumulation of real handoffs. The results do not estimate performance on full repository patches, autonomous tool calling, large active indexes, larger models, or a baseline allowed to read the repository. The reference excerpt gives the model a cleaner prompt, but a run using it can still score worse. Exact answers depend on both **what the index found** and **what the model did with it**. The next useful comparison would use real archived handoffs and a baseline with ordinary repository search. Include competing versions, incomplete coverage, broader rewrites, and multiple seeds or model settings. #### Reproduce locally --- From the `rag-memory-agents` directory, use the project virtual environment with its requirements installed and the configured MiniLM embedding model already cached. The grader uses macOS `sandbox-exec` and the host Python associated with the virtual environment. Start Ollama in a separate terminal if it is not running. ```bash ollama pull qwen3:8b .venv/bin/python scripts/memory_eval/run.py --output /tmp/qwen3-memory-trial.json .venv/bin/python scripts/memory_eval/render.py /tmp/qwen3-memory-trial.json /tmp/qwen3-memory-trial.html ``` Open the generated HTML in a browser. The measurements and model responses are embedded in the page, so browsing the results is offline. The links in its footer resolve when the report is built in the original documentation directory. The checked-in fixture and runner let you inspect the grader independently of the recorded run. #### Verification --- - [x] Installed the requested-size model and completed 27 local Ollama requests using an isolated index and the production memory coordinator. - [x] Verified the nine grading fixtures with reference implementations, and replayed five separately reported edge checks on the saved model outputs. - [x] Ran the existing project suite and linted the new benchmark scripts. All 55 project tests and Ruff checks passed. - [x] Exercised the report in desktop Chrome from a local file, including metric and task-group changes, every case, generated code, retrieved sources, and file links. - [x] Cross-checked the published system and task prompts, the worked example payloads and answers, and all 27 timing and token entries against the saved run.

notes.title: Chunking design decision and strategy
notes.content:
### Chunking design decision and strategy

---

A tested, reliable RAG system is a big step up from a quick first prototype.

Most early demos work fine on day one, then hit hidden snags as time passes and the database grows.

Whether running in production or aiming for efficient and fruitful local usage, getting a few basics right early on helps keep it fast and genuinely useful.

#### Design decisions for `rag-memory-mesh`

---

To reduce silent truncation, semantic dilution, and noisy vectors across code and crawled docs, `rag-memory-mesh` uses six design choices at ingestion and retrieval time.

| Design Dimension | General Principle / Trade-Off | `rag-memory-mesh` Implementation | Why It Works Here |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Token budget | Long inputs can exceed the encoder limit | Default to 900 characters for Markdown chunk bodies and a 2,400-character code split limit | The caps reduce truncation risk. A strict guarantee requires counting tokens after adding any chunk headers. |
| Boundary overlap | A split can separate an explanation from its example | Target 100 characters of overlap within Markdown sections and up to 150 when splitting oversized code | Nearby chunks can share context. Actual overlap depends on the available split boundaries. |
| Markdown and prose | Cutting at a fixed position can break a paragraph or example | Split at `#`, `##`, and `###`, then apply a Markdown-aware recursive splitter | Each chunk carries its heading context. Oversized fenced blocks can still split. |
| Source code | Text-only splits can cut through a declaration or lose its imports | Use Python AST with module imports attached, Tree-sitter for recognized non-Python source, and overlapping UTF-8 text as a fallback | Structural boundaries keep related code together where size permits. A retrieved snippet may still need module state or dependencies. |
| Noise and provenance | Repeated boilerplate takes up index space and obscures relevant text | Prefer pruned Crawl4AI Markdown and carry URL, topic, crawl timestamp, and section metadata into the index | Retrieved text can cite its origin, and the crawl registry tracks freshness. |
| Query and passage alignment | A short question can use different words from the code that answers it | Add symbol and intent headers to Python chunks. Hybrid search combines vector and keyword ranks. Dense search defaults to a maximum distance of `0.38` for `reusable_code` and `0.50` for `research_docs`. | Intent text gives queries more descriptive language to match. The code collection applies a tighter dense cutoff. |

#### Some common chunking pitfalls that helped design decisions

---

##### 1. Token limits and the semantic averaging trap

- Transformer-based embedding models have a limit on how many tokens they process at once. In Sentence Transformers, `model.max_seq_length` exposes that limit.

- Lightweight models like `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` truncate inputs beyond **256 word pieces** by default. Everything past that limit is left out of the embedding. [Model card](https://huggingface.co/sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2#intended-uses)

- `rag-memory-mesh` uses character limits to reduce the risk. A hard token limit would require counting tokens in the final text, including any breadcrumb or filename prefix.

```text
Input tokens    [ first 256 word pieces ][ remaining input ]
Encoder sees   [ first 256 word pieces ]
```

```yaml
chunking:
  md_chunk_size: 900
  md_chunk_overlap: 100
  code_max_chars: 2400
```

##### 2. Semantic dilution — why 5,000 words in one vector can fail

- Even with a long-context embedding model, an entire 5,000-word document can cover too many topics for one vector to represent each one clearly.

- **5,000 words into one vector.** The overall gist may come through, while a specific fact in paragraph 14 can be harder to retrieve.

- **One section at a time.** `rag-memory-mesh` splits Markdown by headings and then splits long sections recursively. Each chunk gets its own vector and carries its section breadcrumb.

```Python
sections = MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter(
    headers_to_split_on=self.HEADERS_TO_SPLIT,
    strip_headers=False,
)
sections = sections.split_text(record.content)

chunk_size=chunk_size if chunk_size is not None else self.chunk_size
chunk_overlap=chunk_overlap if chunk_overlap is not None else self.chunk_overlap
splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter.from_language(
    language=Language.MARKDOWN,
    chunk_size=chunk_size,
    chunk_overlap=chunk_overlap
)
```

##### 3. Problem with using a fixed chunk size everywhere

- Using a single fixed chunk size across file types can break context before a query is even run.

- **Fixed-size splits everywhere.** Tabular data can get cut mid-row, functions can lose their imports and surrounding scope, and long explanations can get detached from their headings.

- **Content-aware chunking.** `rag-memory-mesh` uses Markdown headings, Python AST symbols, and Tree-sitter syntax boundaries for recognized non-Python source. Oversized code, unknown formats, and non-Python syntax errors can use overlapping text splits.

```Python
if is_python:
    chunks = self.code_chunker.chunk(record, max_chars=code_size)

elif is_markdown:
    chunks = self.md_chunker.chunk(record, chunk_size=md_size, chunk_overlap=md_overlap)

else:
    chunks = chunk_source_code(record, max_chars=code_size, grammar=grammar)
```

##### 4. Missing out document metadata

- Embedding raw text without its origin makes it harder to cite sources or tell whether a result is still current.

- **Raw text only.** The search can find a relevant paragraph with no record of which file or section it came from.

- **Metadata attached to each chunk.** `rag-memory-mesh` carries `source_url`, `topic`, and `crawled_at` from the crawl frontmatter, along with a file path and section breadcrumb. Its crawl registry uses indexed timestamps to check freshness.

```Python
metadata = {
    **record.frontmatter,
    "chunk_id": f"{record.filename}::s{sec_idx}_c{sub_idx}::{identity}",
    "source": record.filename,
    "file_path": record.resolved_path,
    "type": "markdown_doc",
    "language": "markdown",
    "section": breadcrumb or "root",
}
```

##### 5. Chunking and embedding data without cleaning

- Chunking raw HTML can flood the vector store with repeated navigation, cookie banners, and sidebars.

- **Uncleaned pages.** Across a documentation site, the same layout text can produce many near-identical chunks that compete with the actual explanations.

- **Clean Markdown before chunking.** `rag-memory-mesh` uses Crawl4AI's pruning filter and prefers `fit_markdown`. It falls back to raw Markdown when the filtered output is empty.

```Python
run_cfg = CrawlerRunConfig(
    cache_mode=CacheMode.BYPASS, page_timeout=opts.page_timeout_ms, verbose=False,
    markdown_generator=DefaultMarkdownGenerator(
        content_filter=PruningContentFilterLXML(threshold=pruning, threshold_type="fixed")
    ),
)
```

##### 6. Asymmetric prefixes (`query:` vs. `passage:`)

In search systems, queries and documents are asymmetric.

- A **query** is short, fragmented, and phrased as a question (*“how do retries back off?”*).

- A **passage** is longer and declarative (*“Each failed attempt doubles the retry delay.”*).

- Some retrieval models are trained with explicit role prefixes such as `query:` and `passage:` to account for that difference.

- In `rag-memory-mesh`, the local query goes directly to `embed_query`. Python chunks carry a symbol name and the first docstring line, or a generated label when there is no docstring. Hybrid search also uses BM25 to match exact identifiers.

```text
Query      "how do retries back off?"
                         │
                         ▼
Python     # Symbol: retry_delay (function)
chunk      # Intent: Each failed attempt doubles the retry delay.
```

```python
doc = ast.get_docstring(node)
intent = doc.strip().splitlines()[0] if doc and doc.strip() else f"Python {sym_type} `{node.name}`"

header = f"# Symbol: {node.name} ({sym_type}) | File: {record.filename}\n# Intent: {intent}\n"
enriched = f"{header}\n{imports_block}\n\n{code_block}" if imports_block else f"{header}\n{code_block}"
```

notes.title: Embedding design decision and model selection
notes.content:
### Embedding design decision and model selection --- An embedding can have the exact number of coordinates expected and still be completely unusable. Silent data corruption happens frequently in RAG systems: - Network hiccups - Half-precision (float16) numerical overflows - Blank PDF extractions - Model timeouts All these can produce vectors filled with `NaN`, `Infinity` or all zeros. If those vectors enter into the index, they will quietly degrade search quality or trigger runtime crashes during similarity queries. #### The ingestion gatekeeper pipeline --- The project's ingestion pipeline validates data at two checkpoints: before calling the embedding model and immediately after receiving the vectors.

##### Checkpoint 1: Reject empty source text early - Idea behind the check- `Never pay to embed nothing`. - It avoid calling model if a document parser extracts an empty string or whitespace-only text from a scanned image or blank page. - Embedding empty string forces the model to generate a fallback vector without semantic meaning (means- wastes API quota and latency). ##### Checkpoint 2: Inspect the returned numbers Validation before normalizing- after model returns a batch of vectors: - Wrong Shape: The response must be a non-empty 2D matrix matching (`batch_size`, `expected_dimension`). - NaN or Infinity: Precision underflows or corrupted model weights can introduce `NaN` or `inf`. A single `NaN` value in an index can corrupt distance calculations across an entire search cluster. - Zero or Near-Zero Length: Cosine similarity measures the angle between two vectors. A vector at the origin `[0.0, 0.0, ...]` has no direction, making its angle to every other vector mathematically undefined. - The "Epsilon Trap" (`length + 1e^-12`): A common approach is adding a tiny number to denominator (vectors / (lengths + 1e^-12)) to prevent division-by-zero errors. This approach is not always reliable, for example, dividing `[0.0, 0.0]` by `1e^-12` still produces `[0.0, 0.0]`. It is dead vector with zero direction that silently pollutes the index. ##### Why Normalize Before Indexing? Recall the cosine similarity formula between a query vector $a$ and a document vector $b$: $$\text{cosine}(a, b) = \frac{\text{dot}(a, b)}{\text{length}(a) \times \text{length}(b)}$$ Normalizing every vector to unit length ($\text{length} = 1.0$) during ingestion turns the denominator into $1 \times 1 = 1$. At query time, cosine similarity reduces to a pure **dot product**: $$\text{cosine}(a, b) = \text{dot}(a, b)$$ This saves the search engine from recomputing square roots and divisions for millions of documents on every user query. #### Embedding model selection --- - Model selection depends on the dataset to be embedded. - MTEB Leaderboard- for getting idea about the performance benchmark for text embedding models. ##### Embedding dimensions and matryoshka models - Embedding dimension: Length of its output array where each number represents a learned latent feature: tone, domain, entity type or syntax. ##### Standard dimensionality tiers | Dimensionality Tier | Example Models | Performance & Resource Trade-off | Best Use Cases | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | 384 Dimensions | `all-MiniLM-L6-v2`, `bge-small-en-v1.5` | Ultra-fast inference and minimal memory footprint | Real-time edge search and large corpora with simple vocabulary | | 768 Dimensions | `all-mpnet-base-v2`, `bge-base-en-v1.5`, `e5-base-v2` | Production sweet spot; balances contextual nuance with manageable RAM usage | General production search and semantic retrieval | | 1024+ Dimensions | `bge-large-en-v1.5`, `e5-large-v2` | Maximum semantic resolution; uses ~2.6x more storage and compute than 384d | Dense legal, medical, or scientific jargon | ##### Matryoshka representation learning (MRL) - Modern models trained with MRL (eg., `nomic-embed-text-v1.5`, `bge-m3`) pack the most important semantic information into the earliest dimensions of the vector and finer details into the later dimensions. - 768-dimensional MRL vector can be sliced down to its first 256 or 128 numbers (followed by L2 normalization) to slash storage costs while retaining over 95% of retrieval accuracy. ##### Top code and technical retrieval models | Model | Type / License | Context Window | Dimensions & Features | Best Use Case | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | voyage-code-3 (Voyage AI / MongoDB) | Hosted API (Proprietary) | 32,000 tokens | Matryoshka (256–2048); supports int8 and binary quantization | Code retrieval across 300+ languages with lower storage costs (also consider Voyage 4 family like voyage-4-large) | | Qwen3-Embedding (0.6B / 4B / 8B) | Open-weight (Apache 2.0) | 32,000 tokens | Matryoshka dimension support; scalable model sizes (0.6B to 8B) | Self-hosted code retrieval; 8B for max GPU accuracy, 0.6B/4B for tight memory budgets | | OpenAI text-embedding-3-large | Hosted API (Proprietary) | 8,191 tokens | Up to 3,072 dimensions; broad ecosystem integration | General-purpose mixed code and documentation search | | BGE-M3 (BAAI) | Open-source (568M params) | 8,192 tokens | Dense, sparse, and multi-vector retrieval in one model | Hybrid search and technical or multilingual repositories | | Other Notable Options (Nomic Embed Code 7B, CodeSage Large V2 1.3B, Gemini Embedding 2, Codestral Embed) | Open-weight & Hosted APIs | Varies by model | Code-specific architectures or multimodal/stack-specific APIs | Specialized code-only indexing or matching existing cloud/API stacks | ##### Selection criteria - Self-hosted vs. API: Self-host Qwen3-Embedding or BGE-M3 for data privacy, zero per-token fees or VPC deployment. Hosted APIs like Voyage OpenAI when you want managed scaling without GPU maintenance. - Context and chunking: Even with 8K–32K context limits, chunking code by function, class or AST boundary usually improves retrieval precision over embedding giant files whole. - Evaluating on my repository: Test candidates on a sample of real queries from codebase (eg, function names, error messages and natural-language intent) before committing to a full index.

notes.title: Source code chunking and embedding strategy
notes.content:
### Source code chunking & embedding strategy

---

Source code has higher token density, strict structural boundaries, and exact identifier requirements that break standard text chunkers. 

**`rag-memory-mesh`** enforces six core rules to keep code chunks accurate, runnable, and searchable.


#### 1. Syntax token density (`code_max_chars: 2400`)

---

* **Pitfall:** Code punctuation (`():{}[]_`) tokenizes at ~2.5 chars/token (vs. ~4.5 in prose). Oversized chunks silently truncate past the encoder's token limit.

* **Fix:** Cap code symbols at **2,400 chars** and split oversized classes along Python syntax separators with a **150-char overlap**.

```python
class PythonAstChunker:
    def __init__(self, max_chars: int = 2400, overlap_chars: int = 150):
        self.max_chars = max_chars
        self.overlap_chars = overlap_chars

    def split_oversized_symbol(self, symbol_source: str) -> list[str]:
        if len(symbol_source) <= self.max_chars:
            return [symbol_source]

        splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter.from_language(
            language=Language.PYTHON,
            chunk_size=self.max_chars,
            chunk_overlap=self.overlap_chars,
        )

        return splitter.split_text(symbol_source)
```


#### 2. Three-tier structural routing

---

* **Pitfall:** Whole-file embeddings dilute specific functions; fixed character cuts slice functions mid-logic; emitting every AST node creates 1-line noise.

* **Fix:** Route Python through `ast` symbol extraction (`PythonAstChunker`), pack ~40 other languages greedily along Tree-sitter top-level nodes (`bisect_right`), and fall back to text blocks on syntax errors.

```python
def pack_syntax_nodes(record: RawFileRecord, root, max_chars: int = 2400) -> list[str]:
    source = record.content.encode("utf-8")
    boundaries, prev_byte, prev_char = [], 0, 0

    for node in root.named_children:
        prev_char += len(source[prev_byte:node.end_byte].decode("utf-8"))
        prev_byte = node.end_byte
        boundaries.append(prev_char)

    chunks, start, next_boundary = [], 0, 0
    while next_boundary < len(boundaries):
        boundary = max(next_boundary, bisect_right(boundaries, start + max_chars) - 1)
        end = boundaries[boundary]
        chunks.append(record.content[start:end])
        start, next_boundary = end, boundary + 1

    return chunks
```


#### 3. Self-contained runnable context

---

* **Pitfall:** Functions extracted mid-file lose their top-level imports and aliases (`np`, `httpx`), leaving retrieved snippets unrunnable.

* **Fix:** Extract all module-level `import` and `from ... import` lines and prepend them to every symbol chunk.

```python
def extract_imports(tree: ast.Module, lines: list[str]) -> tuple[str, list[str]]:
    import_lines, symbols = [], []

    for node in tree.body:
        if isinstance(node, (ast.Import, ast.ImportFrom)) and node.end_lineno:
            import_lines.append("\n".join(lines[node.lineno - 1 : node.end_lineno]))

            for alias in node.names:
                if alias.name != "*":
                    symbols.append(alias.asname or alias.name.split(".")[-1])

    return "\n".join(import_lines), symbols
```


#### 4. Directed code dependency graph

---

* **Pitfall:** Isolated function chunks hide parent classes and helper functions called inside the body.

* **Fix:** Record `inherits`, `calls`, and `imports` edges in SQLite (`CodeGraphStore`) during AST traversal to attach one-hop neighbors at search time.

```python
def extract_edges(node: ast.AST, imported_symbols: set[str]) -> list[tuple[str, str]]:
    edges: list[tuple[str, str]] = []

    if isinstance(node, ast.ClassDef):
        for base in node.bases:
            if isinstance(base, ast.Name):
                edges.append((base.id, "inherits"))

    for child in ast.walk(node):
        if isinstance(child, ast.Call):
            target = (
                child.func.id if isinstance(child.func, ast.Name)
                else child.func.attr if isinstance(child.func, ast.Attribute)
                else None
            )

            if target and target not in _BUILTINS:
                relation = "imports" if target in imported_symbols else "calls"
                edges.append((target, relation))

    return list(dict.fromkeys(edges))
```


#### 5. Hybrid lexical + dense search

---

* **Pitfall:** Vector search matches conceptual intent but blurs exact function names (`retry_delay_v2` vs. `retry_delay_v1`).

* **Fix:** Fuse Chroma vector ranks (60%) and SQLite FTS5 BM25 keyword ranks (40%) using Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF).

```python
def fuse_code_ranks(dense_ranks: dict[str, int], bm25_ranks: dict[str, int], k: int = 60) -> list[tuple[str, float]]:
    scores: dict[str, float] = {}

    for chunk_id in set(dense_ranks) | set(bm25_ranks):
        dense_score = 0.6 / (k + dense_ranks[chunk_id]) if chunk_id in dense_ranks else 0.0
        bm25_score = 0.4 / (k + bm25_ranks[chunk_id]) if chunk_id in bm25_ranks else 0.0
        scores[chunk_id] = dense_score + bm25_score

    return sorted(scores.items(), key=lambda item: item, reverse=True)
```


#### 6. Asymmetric query-to-code alignment

---

* **Pitfall:** Short natural-language queries (*"retry failed HTTP calls"*) drift away from terse code syntax in vector space.

* **Fix:** Frame code chunks with `# File:`, `# Symbol:`, and `# Intent:` headers plus `passage:` / `query:` prefixes, stored in `reusable_code` with a stricter similarity threshold (`0.38`).

```python
def format_code_passage(filename: str, symbol: str, intent: str, imports: str, code: str) -> str:
    header = f"# File: {filename} | Symbol: {symbol}\n# Intent: {intent}"
    body = f"{imports}\n\n{code}".strip() if imports else code.strip()
    return f"passage: {header}\n{body}"

def format_code_query(refined_query: str) -> str:
    return f"query: {refined_query.strip()}"
```

notes.title: Vector database selection
notes.content:
### Vector database selection --- This RAG-memory system is primarily a single-user tool when running on an individual machine. At the same time, it can be deployed over a LAN on a local home server or networked via AWS to support multiple concurrent users. The primary design decisions below assume 1–100 concurrent users, but the comparison below evaluates databases across the full spectrum including high-scale production scenarios. #### Choosing the right database --- **Popular vector databases-** * **Chroma:** Lightweight, Python-first database built for rapid prototyping and local development. * **pgvector:** PostgreSQL extension enabling vector similarity search alongside relational SQL data. * **Qdrant:** High-performance, Rust-based vector engine optimized for speed, filtering, and memory efficiency. * **Weaviate:** Schema-first vector database with native hybrid search and modular AI integrations. * **Pinecone:** Fully managed, serverless cloud vector database built for zero-ops production scale. #### Key selection factors --- **1. Vector volume and scale:** | Vector Volume | Recommended Databases | Key Consideration | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | ≤ 1M vectors | Chroma, pgvector | Work smoothly with minimal setup and low overhead. | | 1M – 50M vectors | Qdrant, pgvector, Weaviate, Pinecone | Handle this range well; filtering performance and ops effort start to matter. | | 50M – 500M+ vectors | Qdrant (clustered with quantization/disk tiers), Pinecone | Prevent high RAM bottlenecks at large scale. |
**2. Hosting and operations:** | Deployment Model | Available Options | Key Consideration | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Managed cloud | Pinecone, Qdrant Cloud, Weaviate Cloud, Chroma Cloud | Minimal maintenance and built-in backups with usage-based billing. | | Self-hosted | Chroma, pgvector, Qdrant, Weaviate | Full data control and lower infrastructure cost at scale, but requires handling updates, scaling, and backups. |
**3. Filtering and hybrid search** | Search Capability | Recommended Databases | Key Consideration | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Strict metadata filtering | Qdrant, Weaviate, pgvector | Qdrant and Weaviate apply filters without hurting search accuracy; pgvector supports full SQL `WHERE` clauses and joins. | | Hybrid search (semantic + keyword) | Weaviate, Qdrant, pgvector | Weaviate and Qdrant support native hybrid queries; pgvector pairs with Postgres full-text search (`tsvector`). |
**4.
